effects.name: Thermal Expansion
effects.description: Materials expand when heated and contract when cooled
applications: Bi-metal strips in thermostats
Expansion joints in bridges
Shrink-fit assembly
effects.quantitative: CTE: steel ~12·10⁻⁶ 1/K, aluminium ~23·10⁻⁶, Invar ~1.2·10⁻⁶, fused silica ~0.5·10⁻⁶; bimetal strip curvature follows the Timoshenko formula; shrink-fit interference typically 0.5–2 ‰ of shaft diameter
effects.limits: Differential CTE is also a failure source: thermal stress, warping, solder-joint cracking; only useful within the material's stable temperature range; anisotropic composites expand differently along axes; repeated cycling can ratchet clearances
effects.source: Timoshenko, S. (1925). Analysis of Bi-Metal Thermostats. J. Opt. Soc. Am. 11(3), 233–255. DOI: 10.1364/JOSA.11.000233; Яворский Б.М., Детлаф А.А. Справочник по физике. М.: Наука, 1968

effects.name: Shape Memory Effect
effects.description: Certain alloys return to their original shape when heated
applications: Shape memory stents
Self-deploying structures
Temperature-activated fasteners
effects.quantitative: NiTi: recoverable strain up to 8% one-way (~4% cyclic); recovery stresses 400–700 MPa; transformation temperatures settable by composition roughly −200…+110°C; thermal hysteresis 20–40 K
effects.limits: Functional fatigue: strain recovery degrades after thousands–millions of cycles; composition and heat treatment control is tight; thermal mass limits actuation frequency; deforms permanently if overheated above the martensite-destabilizing range
effects.source: Buehler, W.J., Gilfrich, J.V., Wiley, R.C. (1963). J. Appl. Phys. 34(5), 1475–1477. DOI: 10.1063/1.1729603

effects.name: Piezoelectric Effect
effects.description: Materials generate electricity when mechanically stressed
applications: Quartz watches
Ultrasonic transducers
Energy harvesting from vibration
effects.quantitative: d-coefficients: quartz ~2.3 pC/N, PZT-5H d33 ≈ 590 pC/N; coupling factor k33 up to ~0.75; Curie temperature of PZT 200–350°C; transducers from 20 kHz to 100 MHz; free strain <0.2%
effects.limits: Poled ceramics depole permanently above the Curie point; charge leaks through finite insulation, so quasi-static signals decay (needs charge amplifier); brittle and hard to integrate in tension; pyroelectric charge can be mistaken for force signal
effects.source: Jaffe, B., Cook, W.R., Jaffe, H. Piezoelectric Ceramics. Academic Press, 1971

effects.name: Electrochromic Effect
effects.description: Materials change color when electric voltage is applied
applications: Smart windows
Anti-glare mirrors
Display technologies
effects.quantitative: WO3 devices: visible transmittance modulates ~5–60%; switching time 5 s to several minutes (area/diffusion limited); memory ≥10⁴–10⁵ cycles; drive voltage ±1–3 V
effects.limits: Slow for large panels (ion diffusion); degradation under UV and over-charge; requires expensive transparent conductors (ITO); tint is not freely color-selectable; sluggish at low temperature
effects.source: Granqvist, C.G. Handbook of Inorganic Electrochromic Materials. Elsevier, 1995

effects.name: Superconductivity
effects.description: Zero electrical resistance at very low temperatures
applications: MRI machines
Maglev trains
Power transmission
effects.quantitative: Tc: NbTi 9.2 K, Nb3Sn 18 K, YBCO 92 K; engineering current density 10⁵–10⁶ A/cm² at 4.2 K in few-tesla fields; MRI magnets routinely 1.5–3 T, research >20 T; Meissner expulsion of B up to Hc1
effects.limits: Cryogenic infrastructure mandatory (near-room-T hydrides need megabar pressures — impractical); quench can destroy magnets without protection; type-II critical field and current limits; AC losses and flux creep remain nonzero
effects.source: Bardeen, J., Cooper, L.N., Schrieffer, J.R. (1957). Theory of Superconductivity. Phys. Rev. 108(5), 1175–1204. DOI: 10.1103/PhysRev.108.1175

effects.name: Aerogel Properties
effects.description: Extremely low density solid with excellent insulation properties
applications: Thermal insulation
Acoustic damping
Lightweight structures
effects.quantitative: Density 3–350 kg/m³ (porosity up to 99.8%); silica aerogel thermal conductivity 0.013–0.020 W/(m·K), below still air (0.026); specific surface area up to ~1000 m²/g
effects.limits: Native silica aerogel is brittle and dusts; hydrophilic variants absorb moisture and shrink; costly at scale; insulation degrades if compressed or wetted; tensile strength low — needs reinforcement
effects.source: Pierre, A.C., Pajonk, G.M. (2002). Chemistry of Aerogels and Their Applications. Chem. Rev. 102(11), 4243–4266. DOI: 10.1021/cr0101306

effects.name: Sonoluminescence
effects.description: Light emission from collapsing bubbles in liquid under sound waves
applications: Sonochemistry
Medical imaging
Cleaning technologies
effects.quantitative: Single-bubble regime: flash width ~30–300 ps, one flash per acoustic cycle (20–40 kHz); hotspot temperature estimated 5,000–15,000 K; collapse pressures ~10⁸ Pa; needs degassed liquid and ~1 atm acoustic drive
effects.limits: Requires clean, degassed liquid and a stably trapped bubble — fragile setup; light output is a vanishing fraction of the acoustic energy (no usable light source); hotspot physics still debated; parametric instabilities destroy the trap
effects.source: Putterman, S.J., Weninger, K.R. (2000). Sonoluminescence: How Bubbles Turn Sound into Light. Annu. Rev. Fluid Mech. 32, 445–476. DOI: 10.1146/annurev.fluid.32.1.445

effects.name: Capillary Action
effects.description: Liquid movement through narrow spaces against gravity
applications: Wick in candles
Plant root systems
Porous media flow
effects.quantitative: Jurin's law h = 2γcosθ/(ρgr); water in glass (γ = 72.8 mN/m, θ ≈ 0°): r = 1 mm → h ≈ 15 mm, r = 10 µm → h ≈ 1.5 m; wicking rate follows Lucas–Washburn √t law
effects.limits: Lift and flow are tiny for large pores; contact-angle hysteresis, trapped bubbles (Jamin effect) and salt deposits block it; surfactants kill the driving pressure difference; transport over long distances is slow
effects.source: de Gennes, P.G. (1985). Wetting: statics and dynamics. Rev. Mod. Phys. 57(3), 827–863. DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.57.827

effects.name: Thermoelectric Effect
effects.description: Direct conversion between temperature differences and electric voltage
applications: Waste heat recovery
Temperature sensors
Portable refrigerators
effects.quantitative: ZT: Bi2Te3 ≈ 1 (commercial), best laboratory materials ≈ 1.4–2; Seebeck coefficient 50–250 µV/K; single-stage Peltier coolers reach ΔT up to 60–70 K with COP 0.3–0.8 (compressors 2–4)
effects.limits: Efficiency far below Carnot once ΔT exceeds ~100 K — poor for bulk power generation; parasitic heat conduction through legs; contact resistances dominate small devices; justified mainly where silence, no moving parts and reliability matter
effects.source: Snyder, G.J., Toberer, E.S. (2008). Complex thermoelectric materials. Nat. Mater. 7, 105–114. DOI: 10.1038/nmat2090

effects.name: Magnetorheological Effect
effects.description: Fluids change viscosity in magnetic fields
applications: Adaptive shock absorbers
Clutches and brakes
Seismic dampers
effects.quantitative: Field-induced yield stress 50–100 kPa at B ≈ 0.8–1 T (an order of magnitude above ER fluids); response <10 ms; off-state viscosity 0.1–1 Pa·s; carbonyl-iron particles 1–10 µm at 20–40 vol%
effects.limits: Sedimentation and 'in-use thickening' shorten service life; holding state consumes power (fail-safe needs spring backup); yield stress ceiling limits clutch torque; working range roughly −40…+150°C
effects.source: Carlson, J.D., Catanzarite, D.M., St. Clair, K.A. (1996). Commercial Magneto-Rheological Fluid Devices. Int. J. Mod. Phys. B 10(23–24), 2857–2865. DOI: 10.1142/S0217979296001306

effects.name: Bioluminescence
effects.description: Light production by living organisms through chemical reactions
applications: Safety lighting
Medical imaging
Environmental monitoring
effects.quantitative: Firefly system quantum yield ~0.15–0.6 (оценки 2018–2021 расходятся; «классические» 0.4–0.6 — верх диапазона); emission spans 450–660 nm across species; ATP/luciferase assays detect down to attomole (10⁻¹⁸ mol) levels; >75% родов открытого океана светятся (Widder 2010: ~80% родов; в литературе встречается 76–80% в зависимости от базиса выборки) of deep-sea animals produce light
effects.limits: Needs continuous supply of ATP/O2/substrate — signal decays; pH- and temperature-sensitive; far too dim for illumination tasks; genetically expressed reporters add minutes-to-hours latency
effects.source: Widder, E.A. (2010). Bioluminescence in the Ocean: Origins of Biological, Chemical, and Ecological Diversity. Science 328(5979), 704–708. DOI: 10.1126/science.1174269

effects.name: Nanoparticle Effects
effects.description: Unique properties of materials at nanoscale
applications: Drug delivery
Catalysis
Sensors
effects.quantitative: Au spheres 13–20 nm: plasmon resonance ≈ 520 nm (wine-red color); melting point of 2–3 nm Au drops from 1337 K toward ~600–800 K; CdSe quantum dots 2–8 nm emit 450–650 nm, tunable by size; specific surface 10–1000 m²/g
effects.limits: Agglomeration destroys the nano-properties; batch-to-batch spread complicates scale-up; toxicity and clearance issues in vivo; quantum size effects vanish above ~10–20 nm (bulk behavior returns)
effects.source: Daniel, M.-C., Astruc, D. (2004). Gold Nanoparticles. Chem. Rev. 104(1), 293–346. DOI: 10.1021/cr030698+

effects.name: Quantum Tunneling
effects.description: Quantum mechanical phenomenon allowing particles to pass through barriers
applications: Scanning tunneling microscopy
Flash memory
Quantum computing
effects.quantitative: Tunneling current decays as exp(−2κz): in STM it changes ~an order of magnitude per 0.1 nm of gap → vertical resolution ~0.01 nm, lateral ~0.1 nm; flash memory uses Fowler–Nordheim tunneling through 8–12 nm SiO2 at ~10–20 V
effects.limits: Needs nanometre gaps — vibration, drift and contamination destroy the signal; exponential sensitivity gives huge current spread across real surfaces; tunnel oxide wear-out limits memory endurance; irrelevant at macroscopic scales (decoherence)
effects.source: Binnig, G., Rohrer, H., Gerber, Ch., Weibel, E. (1982). Surface Studies by Scanning Tunneling Microscopy. Phys. Rev. Lett. 49, 57–61. DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.49.57

effects.name: Electrospinning
effects.description: Production of nanofibers using electric fields
applications: Tissue engineering
Filtration
Composites
effects.quantitative: Fiber diameters ~50–500 nm (tens of nm to a few µm); voltage 5–30 kV at 10–20 cm tip-to-collector; throughput ~0.1–1 g/h per needle; bending (whipping) instability provides most of the jet drawing
effects.limits: Low throughput per jet — needs multi-jet/nozzleless scaling; volatile solvents or melt heating required; bead defects from jet instability; mat cohesion poor without post-processing; humidity and solvent control are critical
effects.source: Reneker, D.H., Yarin, A.L. (2008). Electrospinning jets and polymer nanofibers. Polymer 49(10), 2387–2425. DOI: 10.1016/j.polymer.2008.02.002

effects.name: Magnetocaloric Effect
effects.description: Temperature change in magnetic materials under changing magnetic fields
applications: Magnetic refrigeration
Heat pumps
Sensors
effects.quantitative: Gd at 295 K: adiabatic ΔT ≈ 2.5–3.5 K per 1 T (~5–6 K at 5 T); Gd5Si2Ge2 giant MCE: ΔS ≈ 18–20 J/(kg·K) at 5 T; prototypes reach COP 5–10 at small ΔT but need 1.5–2 T fields
effects.limits: Requires strong fields — permanent-magnet arrays are heavy and expensive; narrow operating window near the transition temperature; hysteresis losses in giant-MCE alloys; heat-switching and regeneration limit cycle frequency
effects.source: Pecharsky, V.K., Gschneidner, K.A. (1997). Giant Magnetocaloric Effect in Gd5(Si2Ge2). Phys. Rev. Lett. 78, 4494–4497. DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.78.4494

effects.name: Latent Heat of Phase Change
effects.description: Substances absorb or release large amounts of heat at nearly constant temperature during melting/freezing/evaporation — a thermal battery
applications: Phase-change material (PCM) heat storage in buildings
Wax thermostatic valves and thermal fuses
Sodium acetate heat pads and freezer packs
Sweating / evaporative cooling of humans and electronics
Ice slurry district cooling
effects.quantitative: Water: 334 kJ/kg fusion, 2257 kJ/kg evaporation; paraffin PCMs 180–250 kJ/kg; salt hydrates 100–200 kJ/kg; charge/discharge nearly isothermal (±1–2 K) — 5–50× the sensible heat of the same mass
effects.limits: PCM thermal conductivity is low (~0.2 W/(m·K)) — needs fins or encapsulation; supercooling and phase segregation degrade cycling; volume change at transition stresses containers; unusable for high heat flux without large exchange area
effects.source: Zalba, B., Marín, J.M., Cabeza, L.F., Mehling, H. (2003). Review on thermal energy storage with phase change. Applied Thermal Engineering 23(3), 251–283. DOI: 10.1016/j.apthermaleng.2002.11.001

effects.name: Regelation
effects.description: Ice melts under pressure and refreezes when pressure is released, letting objects pass through a block of ice near 0°C
applications: Wire cutting through an ice block (classic demonstration)
Snowball and ski-trail snow compaction/sintering
Glacier flow around bedrock obstacles
Ice crystal rounding in clouds
effects.quantitative: Melting point drops only −0.074 K/MPa (Clausius–Clapeyron); 1 kg load on a 0.5 mm wire (σ ≈ 7 MPa) shifts Tm by just −0.5 K — sufficient at 0°C; re-icing happens on the low-pressure side within seconds
effects.limits: Works only within ~1–2 K of the melting point; pressure melting alone cannot explain ice skating (friction heating and surface premelting dominate); fails in very cold or highly porous snow; needs the refreezing side to dump heat to the melting side
effects.source: Яворский Б.М., Детлаф А.А. Справочник по физике. М.: Наука, 1968

effects.name: Thermal Shock (Thermal Stress Resistance)
effects.description: Steep temperature gradients generate stresses that crack brittle materials; resistance ranks by the parameter R = σ(1−ν)/(Eα) and can be exploited (tempering, quenching)
applications: Glass tempering: precompressed surface gives ~4× strength
Steel quench hardening (deliberately rushing through the dangerous zone)
Selecting ceramics for furnaces, kilns and brake discs
Thermal-cycling qualification of solder joints and electronics
effects.quantitative: Critical quench ΔTc ≈ 50–60 K for soda-lime glass, ≈ 200 K for alumina, > 1000 K for fused silica (α ≈ 0.5·10⁻⁶ 1/K); tempered glass carries 100–200 MPa surface compression
effects.limits: High CTE + low conductivity + high stiffness = crack-prone (glass, zirconia); the simple R parameter fails for composites and gradient materials; part thickness couples through the Biot number; ductility invalidates the brittle-material criterion in metals
effects.source: Kingery, W.D. (1955). Factors Affecting Thermal Stress Resistance of Ceramic Materials. J. Am. Ceram. Soc. 38(1), 3–15. DOI: 10.1111/j.1151-2916.1955.tb14545.x

effects.name: Supercooling / Superheating (Metastability)
effects.description: Liquids stay liquid below their freezing point (or gas above boiling point) until nucleation occurs — a metastable store of phase-transition energy and a hazard
applications: Sodium acetate hand warmers with triggered crystallization
Understanding freezing rain and aircraft icing (supercooled droplets)
Controlled nucleation in cryopreservation
Cloud seeding with ice-nucleating agents
effects.quantitative: Homogeneous nucleation limit of water droplets ≈ −38…−40°C; tap water typically supercools only −3…−8°C; sodium acetate trihydrate releases ~264 J/g on demand; superheated water in smooth vessels can exceed 100°C then flash-boil violently
effects.limits: Any dust, scratch, bubble or vibration triggers uncontrolled crystallization; large volumes are practically impossible to hold metastable; long-term storage unreliable (delayed nucleation); superheating bumps are a burn hazard in microwaves
effects.source: Debenedetti, P.G. Metastable Liquids: Concepts and Principles. Princeton University Press, 1996

effects.name: Passive Daytime Radiative Cooling
effects.description: A surface that reflects sunlight and emits strongly in the 8–13 μm atmospheric window dumps heat to space and cools below ambient air temperature
applications: Passive roof coatings reducing air-conditioning load
Photonic cooling layers raising PV panel efficiency
Night dew harvesting and condensation collection
Free cooling for cold-chain and telecom cabinets
effects.quantitative: Atmospheric window 8–13 µm; net cooling power 40–120 W/m²; demonstrated 4.9°C below ambient under 850–900 W/m² direct sun with 97% solar reflection (Raman 2014); night-time sub-ambient drops of ~10 K in dry climates
effects.limits: Needs a clear, dry sky — clouds and humidity close the window; wind convection eats the few-kelvin margin; no cooling indoors or under roofs; useless when parasitic heat fluxes exceed ~100 W/m²; soiling degrades both reflection and emissivity
effects.source: Raman, A.P., Abou Anoma, M., Zhu, L., Rephaeli, E., Fan, S. (2014). Passive radiative cooling below ambient air temperature under direct sunlight. Nature 515, 540–544. DOI: 10.1038/nature13883

effects.name: Thermophoresis (Soret) / Dufour Effect
effects.description: A temperature gradient drives species separation in a mixture (Soret); reciprocally a concentration gradient drives heat flow (Dufour)
applications: Clusius–Dickel thermal diffusion columns for isotope separation
Thermophoretic deposition of soot on cold probes (measurement and filtration)
DNA/protein manipulation in microfluidic thermal gradients
Aerosol sampling and particle-free zones near hot surfaces
effects.quantitative: Soret coefficient S_T ~ 10⁻³–10⁻² K⁻¹ in molecular liquids, up to ~1 K⁻¹ for colloids/polymers; separation grows with applied gradient (typ. 10–100 K/cm); isotope columns needed weeks-to-months of counterflow operation
effects.limits: Extremely slow and weak per stage; natural convection destroys the separation unless the column geometry is used; predictive theory solid only for dilute gases; not competitive with centrifuges or membranes for bulk separations
effects.source: de Groot, S.R., Mazur, P. Non-Equilibrium Thermodynamics. North-Holland, 1962

effects.name: Heat Pipe (Two-Phase Capillary Loop)
effects.description: Sealed pipe where fluid evaporates at the hot end, condenses at the cold end and a capillary wick returns the liquid — near-isothermal heat transport at huge effective conductivity
applications: CPU/laptop coolers and vapor-chamber heat spreaders
Spacecraft thermal control (works without gravity)
Permafrost stabilization thermosyphons on pipelines
Heat-recovery exchangers and cooled furnace panels
effects.quantitative: Effective conductivity 10–100 kW/(m·K) versus copper 0.4 kW/(m·K); conventional designs carry up to ~100 W/cm²; operating range −200…+2000°C (ammonia to alkali metals); temperature drop along the pipe is only a few kelvin
effects.limits: Bounded by capillary, sonic, entrainment and boiling limits; wick types fail when oriented against gravity (pure thermosyphons need gravity); non-condensable gases progressively disable it; freeze–thaw and fluid–wall compatibility degrade over life
effects.source: Grover, G.M., Cotter, T.P., Erickson, G.F. (1964). Structures of Very High Thermal Conductance. J. Appl. Phys. 35(6), 1990–1991. DOI: 10.1063/1.1713792

effects.name: Mechanical Resonance
effects.description: Oscillation amplitude amplifies sharply when the driving frequency matches a natural frequency — a cheap force amplifier and a notorious destroyer
applications: Vibratory sieves and compactors driven near resonance (small motor, large stroke)
Resonant sensing: mass/viscosity shifts frequency (QCM, MEMS gyros, AFM)
Ultrasonic horns and amplitude transformers
Negative case: Tacoma Narrows 1940 (torsional aeroelastic flutter at ~0.2 Hz) — often mis-taught as simple resonance
effects.quantitative: f_n = (1/2π)√(k/m); amplitude gain at resonance ≈ Q (welded steel structures 10–50, precision tuning forks >10⁴); build-up time ~Q/f; Tacoma Narrows collapsed 7 Nov 1940 in ~19 m/s wind
effects.limits: Benefit requires high Q but damping destroys it; narrow band — detunes with temperature, wear and added mass; resonance is crossed during start/stop (transient overshoot); in large structures it is chiefly a failure mode to design out
effects.source: Den Hartog, J.P. Mechanical Vibrations, 4th ed. McGraw-Hill, 1956; Billah, K.Y., Scanlan, R.H. (1991). Am. J. Phys. 59(2), 118–120. DOI: 10.1119/1.16598

effects.name: Gyroscopic Effect / Precession
effects.description: A spinning body resists reorientation and responds to torque by precessing perpendicular to that torque at rate Ω = τ/L — attitude stabilization and rotation sensing
applications: Control moment gyros for spacecraft attitude (ISS uses 4 CMGs, propellant-free)
Ship and drilling-platform roll stabilizers
MEMS vibrating gyros in phones, drones and cars
Bicycle/motorcycle stability and spinning-projectile stabilization
effects.quantitative: Precession rate Ω = τ/(Iω); MEMS gyro bias 0.01–0.1°/s (consumer) vs fibre-optic/ring-laser gyros 0.001–0.01°/h (navigation grade); reactive gyroscopic torque scales with spin speed × angular rate of the frame
effects.limits: Gimbal lock in 2-DOF mounts; bearing friction causes drift; gyroscopic couples in rotors (turbines, aero engines) excite whirling vibration; does not resist translation — attitude only; spinning stores need care at RPM limits
effects.source: Feynman Lectures on Physics Vol. I (1963), ch. 20 'Rotation in space'

effects.name: Tuned Mass Damper (Inertial Damper)
effects.description: A secondary mass-spring-damper tuned to a structure's dominant mode drains vibration energy into itself, suppressing resonance amplitude
applications: Taipei 101: 660 t steel pendulum against typhoon sway
Pedestrian bridge and chimney dampers
Crankshaft and driveline torsional dampers
Stockbridge dampers on power-line conductors
effects.quantitative: Mass ratio μ = 0.5–5% of modal mass; Den Hartog optimum tuning ratio f ≈ 1/(1+μ); adds ~2–4% damping; Taipei 101's 660 t sphere (~0.1% of the ~700 kt tower) cuts typhoon sway by ~40%
effects.limits: Narrow-band: loses effect when the mode shifts (mass change, temperature, ice); adds dead weight at the top of structures; ineffective against broadband random excitation; needs accurate modal model and periodic maintenance of damping elements
effects.source: Den Hartog, J.P. Mechanical Vibrations, 4th ed. McGraw-Hill, 1956

effects.name: Vibrational Conveyance (Vibro-Transport)
effects.description: Asymmetric vibration makes friction act differently in the two stroke halves, ratcheting parts along a track and passively orienting them
applications: Vibratory bowl feeders orienting parts at assembly stations
Vibratory conveyors for hot, abrasive or sticky bulk materials
Vibrating tables for compaction and settling
Linear vibratory feeders and part sorters
effects.quantitative: Typical drive 20–120 Hz (mains-synchronized 50/100 Hz common); amplitude 0.1–3 mm; conveying speed 0.02–0.5 m/s on tracks inclined 20–30° upward; only geometrically 'good' attitudes advance — orientation for free
effects.limits: Noisy (can exceed 80 dB(A)); jams on tangled, springy or magnetic parts; above the throw threshold parts launch and damage; track wear produces abrasive dust; delicate parts suffer impact loading
effects.source: Blekhman, I.I. Vibrational Mechanics: Nonlinear Dynamic Effects, General Approach, Applications. World Scientific, 2000

effects.name: Acoustic Levitation
effects.description: Acoustic radiation pressure traps small objects at standing-wave pressure nodes — contactless holding without container or support
applications: Containerless processing of melts and undercooled droplets
Contactless transport of drops/reagents for chemistry and protein X-ray work
Acoustic tweezer arrays for droplet merging and micro-assembly
Handling of sterile or hazardous samples without contact
effects.quantitative: Object size ≲ λ/2 — at 40 kHz in air (λ ≈ 8.6 mm) that is ~4 mm; trapping needs ~150–160 dB SPL; node spacing λ/2 ≈ 4.3 mm; levitation of ants, ladybugs and small fish demonstrated (Xie 2006)
effects.limits: Practically mm-scale, low-density payloads in air; 150+ dB is power-hungry and hearing-hazardous; node positions fixed by geometry (arrays required to move the payload); air currents or weight beyond trap stiffness drop the object instantly
effects.source: Xie, W.J., Cao, C.D., Lü, Y.J., Hong, Z.Y., Wei, B. (2006). Acoustic method for levitation of small living animals. Appl. Phys. Lett. 89(21), 214102. DOI: 10.1063/1.2396893

effects.name: Doppler Effect
effects.description: Wave frequency shifts in proportion to the relative radial velocity of source and observer — velocity becomes directly measurable
applications: Doppler ultrasound blood-flow imaging (2–15 MHz probes)
Police/automotive radar speed measurement
Laser Doppler velocimetry of flows without seeding probes
Astronomical redshift and radar astronomy
effects.quantitative: Δf/f ≈ v/c for small v; medical ultrasound: blood 0.05–1.5 m/s at 3–10 MHz gives shifts of ~0.3–20 kHz; K-band radar (24.125 GHz) yields ~161 Hz per m/s; redshift z = Δλ/λ sets recession velocity
effects.limits: Responds only to the radial velocity component — tangential motion is invisible; ambiguous targets and multipath in clutter; speed of sound depends on medium temperature (ultrasound calibration); very slow motion gives shifts below oscillator stability
effects.source: Яворский Б.М., Детлаф А.А. Справочник по физике. М.: Наука, 1968

effects.name: Ultrasonic Cleaning
effects.description: Intense ultrasound agitates a liquid into cavitating microbubbles whose collapse scours contaminants off surfaces, including hidden crevices
applications: Jewelry, optics and dental/instrument cleaning
Precision degreasing before plating or coating
PCB flux removal in aqueous or solvent baths
Cleaning of porous and micro-structured surfaces
effects.quantitative: Typical 25–45 kHz (precision baths to 1–2 MHz); power density 10–50 W/L; cavitation bubbles ~10–100 µm; removes sub-micron particles from blind holes; bath optimum ~50–60°C
effects.limits: Shadowing — surfaces not 'seen' by the field clean poorly; cavitation erodes soft metals, plastics and fragile microstructures; degassing and frequency choice are critical; large tanks suffer strong field nonuniformity
effects.source: Mason, T.J. Practical Sonochemistry: User's Guide to Applications in Chemistry and Chemical Engineering. Ellis Horwood, 1991

effects.name: Ultrasonic Welding
effects.description: 20–40 kHz vibration under pressure joins plastics or bonds metal foils by interfacial friction heating in a fraction of a second, without bulk heating
applications: Mass joining of plastic housings, cartridges, toys (cycle < 1 s)
Wire bonding in microelectronics (60–140 kHz)
Ultrasonic additive manufacturing of metal foil layers
Sealing of films, tubes and food packaging
effects.quantitative: Frequency 15–70 kHz (20/40 kHz standard); horn amplitude 10–100 µm; weld time 0.2–2 s; joint footprint per horn up to ~10–20 cm; local interface temperature rise confined to microns of the weld line
effects.limits: Joint and horn sizes limited to centimeters; amorphous plastics need energy-director features; vibration attenuates across the part (near-field only); thick, highly damped or filled materials weld poorly; tooling is part-specific
effects.source: Ensminger, D., Bond, L.J. Ultrasonics: Fundamentals, Technologies, and Applications, 3rd ed. CRC Press, 2011

effects.name: Photoelasticity
effects.description: Stressed transparent materials become birefringent in proportion to stress; polarized light reveals the full internal stress field as fringe patterns
applications: Full-field stress analysis on transparent models
Residual-stress QC of tempered glass and plastic parts
3D 'stress-frozen' models sliced and inspected
Photoelastic coatings on metal parts for surface stress mapping
effects.quantitative: Fringe law (σ1−σ2) = N·f_σ/t; epoxy f_σ ≈ 10–12 kN/(fringe·m) → ~1 MPa per fringe for a 10 mm model; whole-field method locating stress concentrations to within one fringe (~MPa)
effects.limits: Requires transparency or a bonded coating; isoclinic and isochromatic fringes mix — compensation needed to separate them; fringe-order ambiguity at sharp gradients; 3D analysis needs the stress-freezing bake and slicing
effects.source: Dally, J.W., Riley, W.F. Experimental Stress Analysis, 3rd ed. McGraw-Hill, 1991

effects.name: Piezoresistive Effect
effects.description: Semiconductor resistivity changes strongly under mechanical strain — gauge factors ~100× metals — the workhorse of MEMS sensing
applications: Silicon MEMS pressure sensors (automotive, medical, industrial)
Strain gauges in load cells and accelerometers
Cantilever biosensors reading surface stress
Downhole and cryogenic pressure instrumentation
effects.quantitative: Gauge factor: p-Si ≈ 100–200, n-Si ≈ −100…−150, metal foil ≈ 2; MEMS pressure sensors span 0.1–1000 bar full scale with 0.1–1% linearity; standard doping 10¹⁹–10²⁰ cm⁻³
effects.limits: Temperature coefficient of resistance is ~10× the strain signal — bridge compensation mandatory; drift under cycling and packaging stress; diffused sensors limited to ~125–150°C; self-heating at high excitation biases the reading
effects.source: Kanda, Y. (1991). Piezoresistance effect of silicon. Sensors and Actuators A 28(2), 83–91. DOI: 10.1016/0924-4247(91)85017-I

effects.name: Magnetostriction
effects.description: Ferromagnetic materials change shape when magnetized (Joule magnetostriction); the inverse effect turns vibration into magnetic signals
applications: Terfenol-D sonar projectors and high-force actuators
Magnetostrictive position sensors in hydraulic cylinders
Vibration energy harvesting with Galfenol
Negative case: transformer hum (laminate the core to suppress)
effects.quantitative: Saturation magnetostriction λ: Terfenol-D ≈ 1600–2000 ppm, Galfenol ≈ 300–400 ppm, nickel ≈ −33 ppm, polycrystalline iron ≈ −7 ppm; drive fields 50–200 kA/m; response is nonlinear with hysteresis
effects.limits: Eddy-current losses at AC drive (laminate or use ferrites); hysteresis converts to heat and drift; Terfenol-D is brittle and costly (Tb/Dy rare earths) with Curie point ~650 K; stroke is small — lever amplification needed for displacement
effects.source: Bozorth, R.M. Ferromagnetism. Van Nostrand, 1951

effects.name: Elastic Energy Storage (Springs)
effects.description: Elastic deformation stores recoverable mechanical energy (½kx², or σ²V/2E) released later as work — the mechanical battery of bows, watches and springs
applications: Mechanical watch mainsprings
Bows, catapults and spring launchers
Vehicle leaf/coil/torsion-bar suspension
Spring-return actuators and fail-safe valve reset
effects.quantitative: Volumetric density σ²/(2E): spring steel near 1 GPa stress ≈ 2.5 MJ/m³ ≈ 0.3 kJ/kg; a watch mainspring stores ~0.05–0.5 J and runs 40+ h; a compound bow stores ~60–100 J
effects.limits: Stress must stay below the elastic limit — energy density far below chemical storage or flywheels; stress relaxation slowly discharges the store ('self-discharge'); fatigue limits cycle count; large energies demand impractically bulky springs
effects.source: Яворский Б.М., Детлаф А.А. Справочник по физике. М.: Наука, 1968

effects.name: Creep and Stress Relaxation
effects.description: Under sustained stress and elevated temperature solids keep deforming slowly (creep); at held strain the stress decays with time (relaxation)
applications: Turbine-blade alloy design (creep-limited service life)
Bolted-flange preload relaxation analysis
Compensation for cold flow of lead and polymer gaskets
Creep-forming and stress-relief annealing of aircraft skins
effects.quantitative: Significant above ~0.3–0.4 Tm (lead creeps at room temperature); Norton law ε̇ = Aσⁿ·e^(−Q/RT) with n ≈ 3–8; bolt preload loss of 5–30% over years at temperature; design allowables ~1% strain per 10⁵ h
effects.limits: Large scatter — life extrapolation is risky; a small temperature shift changes rate by an order of magnitude; tertiary-stage rupture is hard to predict in service; relaxation silently loosens bolts and gaskets (classic hidden failure)
effects.source: Frost, H.J., Ashby, M.F. Deformation-Mechanism Maps: The Plasticity and Creep of Metals and Ceramics. Pergamon Press, 1982

effects.name: Superelasticity (Pseudoelasticity)
effects.description: Stress-induced martensite in Nitinol produces a large strain plateau that fully recovers on unloading — spring-like travel without any thermal trigger (distinct from shape memory actuation)
applications: Self-expanding vascular stents that recover from kinking
Eyeglass frames that snap back after bending
Orthodontic archwires delivering near-constant force
Steerable guidewires and medical instruments
effects.quantitative: Recoverable strain up to 6–8%; stress plateau 400–800 MPa at T > A_f; loading/unloading hysteresis 200–400 MPa; functional fatigue appears after ~10⁴–10⁵ cycles
effects.limits: Narrow temperature window (roughly up to 50°C above A_f) — effect vanishes outside it; plateau shifts with strain rate (self-heating under cycling); expensive wire processing; not usable for thermal actuation (that is the shape-memory mode)
effects.source: Otsuka, K., Wayman, C.M. (eds.) Shape Memory Materials. Cambridge University Press, 1998

effects.name: Griffith Crack Criterion (Fracture Mechanics)
effects.description: A brittle crack grows when released elastic energy covers the new surface energy: σc = √(2Eγ/πa) — strength is set by flaw size, not by the material alone
applications: Fracture toughness (K1c) testing and material selection
Damage-tolerant inspection intervals (flaw size → cycles → critical size)
Strengthening glass/ceramics by removing flaws (etching, flame polishing)
Leak-before-break design of pressure vessels
effects.quantitative: σc = √(2Eγ/(πa)): glass (E = 70 GPa, γ ≈ 0.3 J/m²) with a 1 µm flaw fails at ≈ 100 MPa instead of the theoretical ~10 GPa; K1c: glass ~0.7, engineering ceramics 1–5, Al alloys 25–35, steels 50–150 MPa·√m
effects.limits: Valid for elastic-brittle behavior only — ductile metals require Irwin/Orowan plastic corrections; assumes a pre-existing sharp crack; subcritical slow crack growth (stress corrosion) undermines the inert assumption in glass/ceramics; geometry and size need LEFM correction factors
effects.source: Griffith, A.A. (1921). The Phenomena of Rupture and Flow in Solids. Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 221, 163–198. DOI: 10.1098/rsta.1921.0006

effects.name: Metal Fatigue (S-N / Wöhler)
effects.description: Cyclic stress far below yield nucleates and grows cracks until sudden failure after N cycles — the dominant delayed-failure mode of machines
applications: S-N design curves and safety factors for rotating parts
Shot peening / nitriding to add compressive residual stress
Damage-tolerant aircraft inspection via crack-growth (da/dN) analysis
Fatigue qualification of welds, springs and bearings
effects.quantitative: Steel endurance limit ≈ 0.4–0.5 UTS (200–500 MPa); aluminum alloys have no true endurance limit; Basquin law σ = σf'(2N)^b with b ≈ −0.05…−0.12; Paris law da/dN = C(ΔK)^m with m ≈ 2–4; typical life scatter ±3×
effects.limits: Huge statistical scatter; sensitive to mean stress, surface finish, size, notches, temperature and corrosion; variable-amplitude loading needs Miner summation, which is inaccurate; the 'endurance limit' disappears under corrosive environments
effects.source: Suresh, S. Fatigue of Materials, 2nd ed. Cambridge University Press, 1998

effects.name: Triboelectric Effect (Contact Electrification)
effects.description: Contact and separation of dissimilar materials transfers electric charge, building kilovolt potentials — a static hazard and, as a TENG, a mechanical-to-electric converter
applications: Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENG) harvesting motion and airflow
Electrostatic spray painting and powder coating
Electrostatic separation of mixed plastics and minerals
Negative case: ESD damage to electronics (wrist straps, antistatic floors)
effects.quantitative: Human body potential from walking on carpet 1.5–25 kV (electronics ESD sensitivity from ~100 V); TENG output: tens–hundreds of volts open-circuit, µA-scale current, demonstrated power density up to ~500 W/m²
effects.limits: Humidity above ~40–50% RH bleeds the charge away; triboelectric-series ranking is unreliable on real surfaces; tiny currents require rectification and storage; charge unpredictability makes process control difficult
effects.source: Fan, F.-R., Tian, Z.-Q., Wang, Z.L. (2012). Flexible triboelectric generator. Nano Energy 1(2), 328–334. DOI: 10.1016/j.nanoen.2012.01.004

effects.name: Gecko Adhesion (Dry Van der Waals Grip)
effects.description: Millions of nanoscale spatulae conform to a surface so weak van der Waals forces sum into kilogram-scale shear grip — no glue, no residue
applications: Reusable dry adhesives and climbing robots
Pick-and-place handling of delicate parts and wafers
Vacuum/space grippers (no outgassing adhesive)
Soft-robotics gripper pads
effects.quantitative: Single seta (~100 µm long, ~5 µm diameter) sustains ≈ 200 µN shear (Autumn 2000); each seta carries 100–1000 spatulae of ~200 nm; projected shear adhesion on smooth glass up to ~1 MPa (10 N/cm²)
effects.limits: Needs shear/preload — normal pull-off is far weaker; fails on rough, wet or dusty surfaces; pads contaminate and rely on self-cleaning steps; synthetic versions lose adhesion after few cycles and at elevated temperature
effects.source: Autumn, K., Liang, Y.A., Hsieh, S.T., Zesch, W., Chan, W.P., Kenny, T.W., Fearing, R., Full, R.J. (2000). Adhesive force of a single gecko foot-hair. Nature 405, 681–685. DOI: 10.1038/35015073

effects.name: Joule–Thomson Effect (Throttling)
effects.description: A real gas passing through a throttle at constant enthalpy cools below its inversion temperature (and heats above it) — the core of gas liquefaction
applications: Linde–Hampson air/nitrogen liquefaction
Joule–Thomson cryocoolers for IR detectors
Gas pressure regulation (valve and regulator frosting as a diagnostic hazard)
Expansion valve of vapor-compression refrigerators
effects.quantitative: µ_JT ≈ +0.2–0.25 K/bar for N2/air at 300 K (cooling); inversion temperatures: N2 621 K, O2 764 K, CO2 ~1500 K, H2 202 K, He 40 K — hydrogen and helium heat up at room temperature and need pre-cooling
effects.limits: Heats gases above their inversion temperature (He, H2, Ne at ambient); zero for an ideal gas; throttling is irreversible — less efficient than an expansion engine/turbine; per-pass ΔT is small, so a recuperative heat exchanger is mandatory
effects.source: Яворский Б.М., Детлаф А.А. Справочник по физике. М.: Наука, 1968

effects.name: Gas Compressibility / Pneumatic Spring
effects.description: Compressed gas stores energy and pushes with stiffness k = γpA²/V — a self-centering 'spring made of nothing', easily adjustable by pressure
applications: Gas struts for lids, hatches and office chairs
Air-spring bellows in truck and bus suspension
Pneumatic cushions and airbags for impact buffering
Hydropneumatic accumulators smoothing pressure pulses
effects.quantitative: Stiffness k = γpA²/V (adiabatic, γ ≈ 1.4 for air); stiffness drifts ~0.33%/K since p ∝ T; isothermal recovery work of air at 200 bar ≈ 50 kJ/kg; struts deliver 100–5000 N
effects.limits: Stiffness is temperature-dependent (cold mornings sag); gas leakage over years requires recharging; adiabatic vs isothermal stiffness differ ~40%; force density below hydraulics; over-stroke ruptures seals
effects.source: Feynman Lectures on Physics Vol. I (1963)

effects.name: Standing Waves and Helmholtz Resonators
effects.description: Bounded media support discrete standing-wave resonances; a cavity-neck (Helmholtz) resonator selects and absorbs one narrow frequency band
applications: Organ pipes, wind instruments and whistles (tone generation)
Reactive mufflers: Helmholtz and quarter-wave side branches tuned to engine tones
Room-mode treatment in studios (bass traps)
Bottle-blowing pitch — cavity geometry encodes frequency
effects.quantitative: f_H = (c/2π)·√(A/(V·L_eff)): 0.5 L bottle with 2 cm × 4 cm neck → ≈ 200 Hz; room modes f = c/2L (3 m room → 57 Hz); 8 ft open organ pipe ≈ 70 Hz; absorber bandwidth set by Q (±10–20% of tuning)
effects.limits: Narrow-band by nature — tuning shifts ~2% per 10 K via sound speed; modes create dead spots elsewhere; resonances in ducts can amplify noise instead of absorbing it; multiple tones demand multiple resonators
effects.source: Kinsler, L.E., Frey, A.R., Coppens, A.B., Sanders, J.V. Fundamentals of Acoustics, 4th ed. Wiley, 2000

effects.name: Echo Ranging / Time-of-Flight Sensing
effects.description: Distance from pulse travel time (d = c·t/2); works in darkness, through opaque media, and images hidden structure
applications: Sonar: depth sounding, fish finding, sub-bottom profiling
Ultrasonic parking sensors and tank level gauges (40 kHz)
Medical B-mode ultrasound imaging (1–15 MHz)
Bat and dolphin biosonar for navigation and prey capture
effects.quantitative: d = c·t/2; sound in water ≈ 1480 m/s → 1 s round trip = 740 m of range; 40 kHz air sensors cover ~0.2–5 m (λ ≈ 8.6 mm); bats use 20–200 kHz and classically avoid wires as thin as ~0.1 mm
effects.limits: Blind zone right after the transmit pulse; specular reflection off angled surfaces misses the receiver; severe high-frequency attenuation in air (order 1 dB/m at 40 kHz); temperature gradients bend the beam; multipath creates ghost targets
effects.source: Urick, R.J. Principles of Underwater Sound, 3rd ed. McGraw-Hill, 1983

effects.name: Acoustic Emission (Damage Monitoring)
effects.description: Rapid local crack growth and deformation radiate transient elastic waves; listening to them reveals active damage growth in real time under load
applications: Structural health monitoring of pressure vessels, tanks and bridges
Proof testing of composite/FRP vessels with AE screening
Tool-wear detection in machining
Leak detection in pipelines and valves
effects.quantitative: Typical band 100 kHz–1 MHz (sensors commonly 20–200 kHz); Kaiser effect: no emission until the previous maximum load is exceeded — an irreversible signature; source location to ~1–5% of sensor spacing; hit rate tracks damage rate
effects.limits: Only growing damage emits — static flaws are silent; attenuation and dispersion complicate location; heavy filtering needed in noisy plants; Kaiser effect blocks re-testing without overloads; corrosion thinning without cracking emits almost nothing
effects.source: ASNT Nondestructive Testing Handbook, Vol. 5: Acoustic Emission Testing, 2nd ed. ASNT, 1987

effects.name: Destructive Interference (Active Noise Control)
effects.description: An anti-phase sound field cancels noise in a zone — field-based 'counter-field' suppression of acoustic harm
applications: Active noise-cancelling headphones (feedforward/feedback ANC)
Active control of duct and HVAC fan tones
Engine-order cancellation in car cabins
Negative case: cancellation zones create louder spots elsewhere (spillover)
effects.quantitative: Effective roughly 20 Hz–1 kHz with 10–40 dB achievable reduction at low frequency; passive absorbers take over above ~1 kHz; the controller must hold amplitude/phase to a few degrees of error at the cancellation point
effects.limits: Works only for low-frequency tones and zone-limited noise; echo paths destabilize feedback ANC; zone of quiet shrinks as frequency rises (spillover); cheap ANC headphones do nothing against mid/high-frequency noise — passive isolation does that
effects.source: Kuo, S.M., Morgan, D.R. (1999). Active noise control: a tutorial review. Proc. IEEE 87(6), 943–973. DOI: 10.1109/5.763310

effects.name: Supercritical Water as Solvent and Oxidation Medium
effects.name_ru: Сверхкритическая вода как растворитель и среда окисления
effects.description: Above its critical point (374 °C, 22.064 MPa) water is a single dense phase whose dielectric constant drops from ~78 to ~5-20: salts and inorganics precipitate out while organics and gases (O2, CO2) become fully miscible, so water acts simultaneously as solvent, reactant and oxidizing reaction medium.
applications: Supercritical water oxidation (SCWO) of hazardous organic waste (>99.99% destruction of dioxins, chemical agents) without NOx/SOx emissions
Hydrothermal gasification of wet biomass and sludge to H2/CH4
Continuous hydrothermal flow synthesis of oxide nanopowders (ZrO2, BaTiO3)
Salt-rejecting coolant in supercritical water reactors (GEN-IV)
Selective precipitation of inorganics from organic feeds (desalting)
effects.quantitative: Critical point: 374.0 °C, 22.064 MPa, critical density 322 kg/m3; SCWO at 500-650 °C, 23-28 MPa gives >99.99% organic destruction with residence times <1 min; ionic product of water falls 2-3 orders of magnitude; NaCl solubility drops to ppm level in the SC region, causing salt plugging.
effects.limits: Severe corrosion (Cl- and SO4^2- accelerate attack); salt deposition plugs reactors and requires pressure/temperature ramps or scrapers; energy cost of heating and pressurizing the feed; catalysts usually needed to destroy ammonia; materials for >600 °C/25 MPa are expensive.
effects.source: Kritzer, P., Dinjus, E., An assessment of supercritical water oxidation (SCWO), Chemical Engineering Journal (2001), DOI 10.1016/S1385-8947(00)00255-2

effects.name: Aluminum-Water Hydrogen Generation
effects.description: Bulk aluminium is protected by a passive Al2O3 film and does not react with water below ~280 °C; once the oxide is defeated (alkali solution, Ga-In alloying, ball milling, nanoscale powder or high-pressure steam), the exothermic reaction 2Al + 6H2O -> 2Al(OH)3 + 3H2 releases hydrogen even at room temperature.
applications: On-demand hydrogen generation for fuel cells (portable and backup power)
Aluminium as a recyclable solid hydrogen carrier (H2 from waste Al scrap)
Al-water steam propulsion and underwater power units
Rapid reactivation of supply chains for emergency hydrogen supply
effects.quantitative: Theoretical yield 1244 L H2 (STP) per kg Al (3 mol H2 per mol Al); reaction exothermic (~426 kJ/mol Al with liquid water); bulk Al passivated below ~280 °C in pure water; Ga-In-activated or ball-milled Al reacts at 20-80 °C with near-quantitative conversion in minutes.
effects.limits: Passivation layer must be continuously removed; alkali activators are consumed and Ga/In alloying metals are hard to recycle; product Al(OH)3 slurry must be regenerated by energy-intensive electrolysis (round-trip efficiency ~30-50%); heat and slurry fouling management required.
effects.source: Yavor, Y., Goroshin, S., Bergthorson, J.M., Frost, D.L., Comparative reactivity of industrial metal powders with water for hydrogen production, International Journal of Hydrogen Energy (2015), DOI 10.1016/j.ijhydene.2014.11.075

effects.name: Hydrothermal Synthesis
effects.description: Water at 100-400 °C under autogenous pressure acts as a reactive crystallization medium: solubility and chemical reactivity of many oxides rise steeply, enabling single crystals (quartz, zeolites) and oxide phases that are unreachable by dry high-temperature routes.
applications: Industrial growth of synthetic quartz and zeolites
Continuous hydrothermal flow synthesis (CHFS) of nano-oxides (ZrO2, LiFePO4, BaTiO3)
Hydrothermal carbonization (HTC) of biomass to carbonaceous chars
Hydrothermal leaching and oxidation of ores and hazardous wastes
Simulation of geochemical mineral formation
effects.quantitative: Typical window 120-400 °C at saturated-water pressure up to ~30 MPa; zeolites crystallize at 80-200 °C; quartz growth at 330-400 °C and 70-140 MPa; CHFS mixers heat the feed above 374 °C in <10 s; crystal growth rates scale strongly with temperature (solubility doubling per tens of K).
effects.limits: Batch autoclaves are slow (hours-days) and opaque (no in-situ observation); pressure window restricts solvent chemistry; continuous reactors struggle with solids handling and clogging; autoclave safety at high fill ratios.
effects.source: Byrappa, K., Yoshimura, M., Handbook of Hydrothermal Technology, 2nd ed., William Andrew (2013)

effects.name: Supercritical CO2 as Tunable Solvent
effects.description: CO2 above 31.1 °C and 7.38 MPa is a tunable, non-toxic, non-flammable solvent whose dissolving power follows its density: raising pressure turns it from weak gas into liquid-like solvent, letting it extract caffeine, degrease parts and dry gels without leaving any residue.
applications: Industrial caffeine decaffeination of coffee and tea (Zosel process)
Supercritical drying of silica aerogels - eliminating the liquid-vapor interface so the gel network does not collapse (pairs with the aerogel effect)
Precision degreasing of medical/aerospace parts instead of CFC/halogenated solvents
Fractionation of natural oils and hop/plant extracts
sCO2 Brayton power cycles (same fluid state, energy function)
effects.quantitative: Critical point 31.1 °C, 7.38 MPa; solvent power roughly proportional to density (600-950 kg/m3 between 8 and 20 MPa); coffee decaffeination at ~60-90 °C and 20-30 MPa; aerogel drying at 8-10 MPa above Tc; naphthalene solubility rises 10^3-10^4-fold from 80 to 200 bar.
effects.limits: Poor solvent for polar and ionic species (co-solvents like ethanol needed); high-pressure equipment cost (15-30 MPa class); sudden depressurization precipitates solutes and clogs nozzles; viscosity-diffusion advantages fade for viscous feeds.
effects.source: Zosel, K., Separation with supercritical gases: practical applications, Angewandte Chemie International Edition in English (1978), DOI 10.1002/anie.197807021

effects.name: Cavitation and Cavitation Erosion
effects.description: When local static pressure falls below vapor pressure (or ultrasonic tension exceeds it), vapor bubbles nucleate and then collapse violently, generating micro-jets and shock waves with local pressures of hundreds of MPa and temperatures of thousands of K - used for cleaning, dispersion and sonochemistry, destructive for propellers and impellers.
applications: Ultrasonic and hydrodynamic cavitating reactors for wastewater treatment (OH-radical generation)
Homogenization and dispersion (nanoemulsions, milk, slurries)
Cleaning of parts via controlled bubble collapse
Cavitating waterjets for cutting and rock excavation
Design margins (NPSH) to prevent impeller/propeller erosion
effects.quantitative: Bubble collapse produces local pressures ~100-1000 MPa and hot-spot temperatures ~3000-10000 K; Rayleigh collapse time tR ~ 0.915 R0 sqrt(rho/dP) (10 um bubble, 1 atm -> ~1 us); onset governed by cavitation number sigma = (p - pv)/(0.5 rho U^2) < 1; marine propeller erosion risk above tip speeds of 15-20 m/s.
effects.limits: Needs deliberate pressure drop or strong ultrasound (energy-hungry); erosion of nearby solids (sacrificial coatings, material selection); sonochemical yields scale poorly to industrial volumes; bubble clouds behave chaotically and are hard to predict; collapse energy delivered only within ~1 bubble radius of a surface.
effects.source: Brennen, C.E., Cavitation and Bubble Dynamics, Oxford University Press (1995); classic: Rayleigh, L., Phil. Mag. (1917)

effects.name: Water Hammer (Joukowsky Effect)
effects.description: A sudden change of flow velocity in a pipe (valve slam, pump trip) converts kinetic energy into a pressure wave travelling at the speed of sound of the liquid-pipe system; by the Joukowsky law dp = rho*c*dv, 1 m/s of velocity change in water gives ~10 bar.
applications: Hydraulic ram pumps that lift water uphill using their own flow energy, no external power
Design of surge protection: air chambers, surge tanks, relief valves, slow-closing valves
Transient-based pipeline leak detection and condition assessment
Pulse loading for pipeline cleaning and pigging operations
effects.quantitative: Joukowsky dp = rho*c*dv; wave speed c ~ 1200-1400 m/s in water-filled steel pipes (elasticity of pipe reduces it); critical closure time 2L/c (1 km line -> ~1.5-2.5 s); ram pumps deliver 10-20% of the drive flow to heights up to 10-20 times the source fall.
effects.limits: Harmful in networks: pipe rupture, fatigue, water-column separation with subsequent cavitation; slow closures (>2L/c) need full elastic analysis; entrained gas changes wave speed unpredictably; ram pumps work only with a steady falling source flow.
effects.source: Ghidaoui, M.S., Zhao, M., McInnis, D.A., Axworthy, D.H., A Review of Water Hammer Theory and Practice, Applied Mechanics Reviews (2005), DOI 10.1115/1.1828050; classic: Joukowski, N.E., Mem. Acad. Imp. Sci. St.-Petersbourg (1900)

effects.name: Leidenfrost Effect
effects.description: Above the Leidenfrost temperature a volatile liquid no longer wets a hot surface: a persistent vapor film thermally insulates it, letting droplets skitter nearly frictionlessly and shielding solids from burnout, while texture-guided films can propel droplets without pumps.
applications: Controlled quenching in metallurgy (managing the nucleate-to-film-boiling transition to avoid soft spots)
Safe handling and spill behavior of cryogens (LN2 droplets skitter on floors)
Self-propelled droplet transport on ratcheted/structured hot surfaces (pumpless microtransport)
Steam-explosion and fuel-coolant interaction safety analysis (nuclear, metallurgy)
effects.quantitative: Leidenfrost point for water on polished metals ~220-280 °C (strongly surface- and droplet-size dependent); supporting vapor film ~10-200 um thick; droplet lifetime above the LFP is tens of times longer than just below it; LN2 shows a Leidenfrost state down to ~-180 °C; ratchet textures drive droplets at cm/s speeds.
effects.limits: Transition point shifts by 100+ K with roughness, contamination and droplet size; the vapor film is an insulator - unusable for high-heat-flux cooling; film boiling in quenching causes non-uniform hardness and distortion; unstable between regimes (hysteresis).
effects.source: Bernardin, J.D., Mudawar, I., The Leidenfrost Point: Experimental Study and Assessment of Existing Models, Journal of Heat Transfer (1999), DOI 10.1115/1.2826080; classic: Leidenfrost, J.G., De aquae communis nonnullis qualitatibus tractatus (1756)

effects.name: Critical Heat Flux (Boiling Crisis)
effects.description: As wall superheat or heat flux rises, vigorous nucleate boiling abruptly gives way to an insulating vapor film at the critical heat flux: wall temperature jumps by hundreds of K within milliseconds and can melt the heater - CHF defines the safety ceiling of water-cooled reactors and high-power electronics cooling.
applications: Thermal design limits of nuclear reactor cores (DNB / dryout margins)
Two-phase cooling of high-power electronics and laser diodes (safe operating envelope)
Quench process control in metallurgy
CHF enhancement with porous/nanostructured coatings (2-3x margin gain)
Fuel-coolant interaction (steam explosion) analysis
effects.quantitative: Pool boiling water CHF at 1 atm ~1.0-1.3 MW/m2 (Zuber hydrodynamic limit q ~ 0.13 rho_g h_fg (sigma g drho/rho_g^2)^0.25); after the crisis the wall superheat jumps 100-500 K; microporous coatings raise CHF to ~2-3 MW/m2; flow-boiling CHF in reactor channels ~1-5 MW/m2 depending on pressure and quality.
effects.limits: Even look-up tables predict CHF with +-20-30% uncertainty; strong dependence on geometry, pressure, quality, dissolved gases and surface finish; film boiling is thermally unsustainable for most materials; enhancement coatings age and foul.
effects.source: Dhir, V.K., Boiling Heat Transfer, Annual Review of Fluid Mechanics (1998), DOI 10.1146/annurev.fluid.30.1.365; classic: Zuber, N., PhD thesis, UCLA (1959)

effects.name: Superfluidity of Helium-4 (He-II)
effects.description: Below the lambda point (2.17 K) liquid He-4 flows with effectively zero viscosity through microchannels, creeps as a Rollin film up container walls and out of open vessels, and conducts heat as a propagating wave (second sound) - a frictionless leak-and-heat medium with pumpless fountain transport.
applications: Cooling of the LHC superconducting magnet lattice at 1.9 K (He-II bath)
Second-sound sensors for fast quench localization in superconducting magnets
Fountain-effect pumps with no moving parts for cryogenic circulation
Cryogenic infrared detector assemblies (space telescopes)
Ultra-low-friction model systems and quantum fluid research
effects.quantitative: Lambda transition at 2.17 K (saturated vapor pressure); measured viscosity upper bound <10^-12 Pa*s; Rollin film ~10-50 nm creeps over walls unaided; second sound velocity ~20 m/s; effective thermal conductivity of turbulent He-II up to 10^4-10^5 W/(m*K), ~1000x copper; fountain pressure ~0.1 MPa per 1 K temperature difference.
effects.limits: Exists only below 2.17 K for He-4 (He-3 becomes superfluid at ~2.5 mK); requires full cryogenic infrastructure; creeps out of any imperfect seal (leaks everywhere); superfluidity breaks down above a critical velocity (vortices appear); fountain effect needs a heat leak to sustain flow.
effects.source: Kapitza, P., Viscosity of liquid helium below the lambda-point, Nature (1938), DOI 10.1038/141074a0

effects.name: Shear Thickening (Dilatancy)
effects.description: Dense particle suspensions (cornstarch-water, silica in ethylene glycol) suddenly stiffen above a critical shear rate as hydrodynamic and contact forces assemble jammed particle clusters - viscosity can jump by orders of magnitude, so the medium stays soft at rest and rigid under impact.
applications: Liquid armor: STF-impregnated Kevlar fabrics for stab and ballistic protection
Impact-activated dampers and recoil absorbers
Adaptive robotic grippers that stiffen on contact with the object
Sports padding and energy-absorbing footwear
Tunable clutches and soft-stopping couplings
effects.quantitative: Onset typically at shear rates 10^2-10^3 1/s for 40-55 vol% suspensions; viscosity jump 10^2-10^4x; STF-treated aramid fabrics show several-fold higher energy absorption in stab tests; effect is reversible but degrades slowly over thousands of shear cycles.
effects.limits: Particle sedimentation and agglomeration over storage; requires high solids loading (heavy); above the jump the material can behave momentarily brittle; sensitive to temperature, pH and particle size distribution; poor for sustained static loads (needs shear to activate).
effects.source: Barnes, H.A., Shear-thickening (dilatancy) in suspensions of nonaggregating solid particles, Journal of Rheology (1989), DOI 10.1122/1.550072

effects.name: Thixotropy
effects.description: Time-dependent structural breakdown under shear and slow rebuild at rest: a gel liquefies while stirred or pumped and regains gel strength when standing - fluid when worked, self-supporting when idle.
applications: Anti-sag paints: brushable at high shear, no dripping at rest
Drilling muds that gel to suspend cuttings whenever pumps stop
3D-printing inks and pastes that extrude easily then hold shape
Anti-settling battery electrolyte gels and suspension fertilizers
Food dispensing (ketchup, mayonnaise) and consumer products
effects.quantitative: Viscosity drops 10-10^3x under shear; structural recovery times range 0.1-10 min for paints to tens of minutes for drilling muds (10-min gel strengths ~5-15 Pa); characterized by thixotropic hysteresis loop area in flow curves.
effects.limits: Recovery kinetics are protocol- and composition-dependent (hard to predict); repeated cycling can cause irreversible flocculation or aging; rheometer characterization is ambiguous; not suited for fast impact loading (that is the dilatancy domain).
effects.source: Mewis, J., Wagner, N.J., Thixotropy, Advances in Colloid and Interface Science (2009), DOI 10.1016/j.cis.2008.09.005

effects.name: Weissenberg Effect (Rod Climbing)
effects.description: Viscoelastic fluids develop large first normal stress differences in shear flow: when stirred, the hoop stress squeezes the fluid inward, making it climb the rotating shaft instead of forming the hollow a Newtonian liquid would - a visible signature of elasticity in the liquid.
applications: Rheometric detection of normal stresses (Weissenberg rheogoniometer principle)
In-process QC of polymer melts, doughs and bio-polymer solutions (climbing = elastic)
Design caution for stirred tanks and screw pumps handling viscoelastic media (melt fracture, shaft climbing)
Transport of viscoelastic inks in additive manufacturing
effects.quantitative: Climbing height scales with the first normal stress difference N1 = Psi1*gamma_dot^2; visible for polymer solutions above gamma_dot ~ 10 1/s; typical N1 for 2% polyacrylamide solutions 10-100 Pa at 10-100 1/s; historical Weissenberg rheogoniometer (from 1948) measured N1 via torque and normal force.
effects.limits: Requires elasticity (N1 > 0) - absent in Newtonian liquids; inertial secondary flow can compete and reverse the effect at high rotation; free-surface irregularities and fracture of the meniscus at high rates; climbing height is not a calibrated N1 meter without full rheometry.
effects.source: Weissenberg, K., A continuum theory of rheological phenomena, Nature (1947), DOI 10.1038/159310a0

effects.name: Electroosmosis / EHD Pumping
effects.description: An applied electric field drags the diffuse ion layer of the electric double layer at a charged solid-liquid interface, moving the whole liquid column through capillaries or porous media with no moving parts; in dielectric liquids, field-emitted ions transfer momentum instead (EHD ion-drag pumping).
applications: Lab-on-chip and capillary electrophoresis pumping (plug flow, no valves)
Electrokinetic remediation of clays and soils: extracting heavy metals where hydraulic pumping fails (low permeability)
Electroosmotic dewatering of sludge, peat and wood
EHD micro-pumps for chip cooling with dielectric fluids
Paper-based microfluidics and wicking devices with field-actuated flow
effects.quantitative: Flow mobility mu_eo = eps*zeta/eta ~ (2-5)*10^-8 m2/(V*s) for water in glass; fields of 100-1000 V/cm drive 0.1-3 mm/s in micrometer channels (flat plug-flow profile, no Poiseuille parabola); electrokinetic soil remediation reports >80-90% removal of mobile Cu/Cd from kaolinite in weeks.
effects.limits: Needs a charged interface and conductive liquid (dielectrics require ion-drag variant with low efficiency); Joule heating at high fields; pH/buffer chemistry shifts zeta potential; electrode electrolysis generates gas bubbles; high-voltage safety.
effects.source: Rice, C.L., Whitehead, R., Electrokinetic Flow in a Narrow Cylindrical Capillary, Journal of Physical Chemistry (1965), DOI 10.1021/j100895a062; classic: Reuss, F.F., Mem. Soc. Imperiale Naturalistes de Moscou (1809)

effects.name: Marangoni Effect (Thermocapillary Convection)
effects.description: Gradients of surface tension along a liquid interface (from temperature or surfactant concentration differences) pull surface flow toward higher surface tension, organizing convection cells and driving droplet motion with no moving parts - surface tension acting as a pump.
applications: Weld pool control in laser welding and remelting (Marangoni convection shapes the bead and redistributes alloying elements)
Single-crystal growth (Czochralski, float-zone): suppressing striations from melt convection
Digital microfluidics: surface-tension-gradient pumping and droplet steering
Boiling surface redesign: Marangoni flow re-wets dry spots and delays dryout
Self-assembly of thin coatings (Benard cells control drying patterns)
effects.quantitative: Onset of Benard-Marangoni convection at Marangoni number Ma = (sigma_T*dT*L)/(mu*alpha) > ~80; water: sigma_T ~ -1.5*10^-4 N/(m*K); characteristic velocity ~ sigma_T*dT/mu (dT = 5 K over 1 mm gives ~0.1 m/s scale); works in microgravity where buoyancy cannot.
effects.limits: Surfactants instantly kill it (they clamp surface tension); acts only at free surfaces/interfaces - no effect in full pipes; in large pools buoyancy competes and destabilizes; sensitive to contamination and oxide films on melts.
effects.source: Scriven, L.E., Sternling, C.V., The Marangoni Effects, Nature (1960), DOI 10.1038/187186a0

effects.name: Coanda Effect
effects.description: A jet emerging close to a convex surface stays attached and follows the wall: entrainment of ambient fluid creates low pressure that pins the jet, enabling flow guidance and fluidic switching with no moving parts.
applications: Fluidic logic gates, bistable amplifiers and fluidic oscillators (no moving parts, radiation-hard)
Circulation-control wings and blown flaps (jet over trailing edge augments lift)
Bladeless fans and HVAC diffusers (annular jet clings and entrains room air)
Air curtains and burner flame guidance (safety-relevant attachment)
Spray coating and paint application with wall-following jets
effects.quantitative: Attachment occurs when the wall lies within a few nozzle widths of the jet; reattachment length after a step is 3-6 nozzle widths; jets follow curved walls turning up to ~70-90 deg; fluidic oscillators sweep at 0.1-1000 Hz depending on scale; attached-jet thrust augmentation ~1.3-1.6 in fan applications.
effects.limits: Sensitive to crosswinds and ambient currents (blown flaps lose benefit in gusts); requires proximity to a surface; hysteresis between attached and separated states; extra skin friction and heat load on the wall; marginally stable with Reynolds number changes.
effects.source: Reba, I., Applications of the Coanda Effect, Scientific American 214(6) (1966); classic: Coanda, H., French Patent 792-754 (1936)

effects.name: Karman Vortex Street and Magnus Effect
effects.name_ru: Вихревая дорожка Кармана и эффект Магнуса
effects.description: Bluff bodies in crossflow shed periodic vortices at Strouhal frequency f ~ 0.2*U/D (usable as flow meters, dangerous as VIV), while a spinning body in a stream generates transverse lift via asymmetric circulation (Magnus effect) - vortex behavior made measurable and controllable.
applications: Vortex-shedding flowmeters (bluff body + frequency counting, ~0.5-1% accuracy)
VIV suppression for offshore risers, chimneys and bridge cables (helical strakes, fairings)
Flettner rotor ships and wind-assisted propulsion (Magnus lift)
Aeolian tone suppression on power lines (Stockbridge dampers) and acoustic diagnostics of flows
Ball sports aerodynamics and spinning-projectile ballistics
effects.quantitative: Strouhal number St = fD/U ~ 0.2 for a circular cylinder from Re 300 to 3*10^5; VIV lock-in drives vibration amplitudes up to ~1 body diameter; Magnus lift coefficients of 4-10 for rotating cylinders (vs ~1-1.5 for conventional wings); a 50 mm power line at 10 m/s sheds at ~40 Hz (audible hum).
effects.limits: Lock-in resonance is narrow but destructive (fatigue); shedding becomes chaotic above Re ~ 3.5*10^6 (supercritical regime); Magnus lift collapses at high spin ratios (>2-3) and adds drag; flowmeters need sufficient upstream straight piping.
effects.source: Williamson, C.H.K., Govardhan, R., Vortex-Induced Vibrations, Annual Review of Fluid Mechanics (2004), DOI 10.1146/annurev.fluid.36.050802.122138; classics: von Karman, T., Nachr. Ges. Wiss. Gottingen (1911); Magnus, G., Ann. Phys. (1852)

effects.name: Ferrofluid (Ferro-Magnetic Liquid)
effects.description: A colloidal suspension of ~10 nm superparamagnetic nanoparticles in a carrier liquid remains fully liquid yet obeys magnetic fields - forming Rosensweig spikes, sealing rotation gaps and wetting surfaces; unlike magnetorheological fluids (micron particles, solid yield stress), it stays fluid and can be shaped precisely by weak fields.
applications: Rotary-shaft vacuum and hermetic seals in hard drives and semiconductor equipment (zero-wear, leak-free)
Voice-coil damping and centering in loudspeakers (viscosity + magnetic centering in one liquid)
Magnetically guided drug delivery and tumor hyperthermia (magnetite cores)
Magnetic-domain visualization (ferrofluid patterns on recording media)
Inclinometers and accelerometers using magnetic liquid position sensing
effects.quantitative: Particle diameter 3-15 nm (superparamagnetic, no remanence); saturation magnetization 10-60 kA/m (magnetite-based); normal-field Rosensweig instability spike spacing ~5-10 mm for typical fluids; rotary seals hold 20-100 kPa per stage, stacked stages reach >1 MPa; viscosity 2-500 mPa*s tunable by carrier and loading.
effects.limits: Magnetic forces are far smaller than in MR fluids (no solid-chain yield stress); particle agglomeration and surfactant degradation with time; carrier evaporation; temperature limits of the carrier liquid; costly materials.
effects.source: Rosensweig, R.E., Ferrohydrodynamics, Cambridge University Press (1985); patent: Papell, S.S., US Patent 3,215,572 (1965)

effects.name: Osmosis and Reverse Osmosis
effects.description: Water crosses a semipermeable membrane from dilute to concentrated solution under osmotic pressure (seawater ~27 bar); applying pressure above the osmotic pressure reverses the flow, rejecting >99% of dissolved salts and pathogens - concentration-driven separation and, conversely, pressure recovery from salinity gradients.
applications: Seawater and brackish desalination (the dominant world technology)
Hemodialysis and pure-water supply for medical and semiconductor use
Food and juice concentration at low temperature (no thermal damage)
Pressure-retarded osmosis / blue energy: power from river-sea salinity gradients
Forward osmosis for water reclamation and nutrient-dense feed concentration
effects.quantitative: Seawater osmotic pressure ~27 bar (35 g/L salts); SWRO operates at 55-80 bar, brackish at 10-25 bar; modern membranes reject 99.7-99.85% of salts; specific energy 2.5-4 kWh/m3 against a thermodynamic minimum ~1.06 kWh/m3 at 50% recovery; typical fluxes 10-40 L/(m2*h).
effects.limits: Fouling and scaling demand extensive pretreatment; polyamide membranes degrade with chlorine; brine disposal is an environmental constraint; membrane compaction at high pressure; osmotic power prototypes (Statkraft) closed for low economic efficiency at current membrane performance.
effects.source: Elimelech, M., Phillip, W.A., The Future of Seawater Desalination: Energy, Technology, and the Environment, Science (2011), DOI 10.1126/science.1200488; classic: Loeb, S., Sourirajan, S., Advances in Chemistry Series 38, ACS (1963)

effects.name: Gas Hydrates (Clathrates) and Self-Preservation
effects.description: Water forms solid cage compounds trapping gas molecules (CH4, CO2) at moderate pressure and low temperature: 1 m3 of methane hydrate holds ~164 m3 of gas at STP - a pipeline-plugging hazard, a solid gas-storage medium, a desalination-by-crystallization route, and it dissociates anomalously slowly just below 0 °C (self-preservation by an ice shell).
applications: Hydrate plug prevention in subsea pipelines (thermodynamic inhibitors MEG/MeOH, depressurization)
Solid-state storage and transport of natural and associated gas (SNG hydrate technology)
Desalination by hydrate formation-melting (salt excluded from the clathrate lattice)
CO2 sequestration as hydrate and CO2-CH4 exchange in sediments
Production from natural hydrate deposits (Messoyakha, Nankai Trough trials)
effects.quantitative: Methane hydrate stable at 0-5 °C under ~2.6-6 MPa; 1 volume hydrate = ~164 volumes gas (STP) + 0.8 volumes water; self-preservation window -20 to 0 °C: dissociation rate drops 10-100x (maximum near 268 K); wet-gas pipelines risk plugging at 0-20 °C above a few MPa.
effects.limits: Slow formation without promoters (THF, TBAB) and poor gas-liquid contact; large latent heats must be moved in/out; sand and matrix complicate production; decompression of plugs is an explosion hazard; low volumetric energy density compared with LNG.
effects.source: Sloan, E.D., Koh, C.A., Clathrate Hydrates of Natural Gases, 3rd ed., CRC Press (2008); Stern, L.A., Circone, S., Kirby, S.H., Durham, W.B., Anomalous Preservation of Pure Methane Hydrate at 1 atm, Energy & Fuels (2001), DOI 10.1021/ef000237a

effects.name: Toms Effect (Polymer Drag Reduction)
effects.description: Parts-per-million doses of long-chain polymers in turbulent flow damp near-wall momentum exchange and cut frictional drag by up to ~80% without measurably changing bulk viscosity - a molecular-level lubrication of turbulence.
applications: Long-distance crude oil pipelines (dosing 5-50 ppm boosts throughput 30-50%)
Fire-fighting hoses (longer throw at the same pump power)
District heating and cooling water networks (lower pumping cost)
Marine hull drag reduction experiments and fast boat fuel savings
Sewer and process line hydraulic capacity upgrades without new piping
effects.quantitative: 10-100 ppm polyethylene oxide or polyacrylamide reduce turbulent friction up to 70-80% (Virk maximum drag reduction asymptote); effective in fully turbulent flow above Re ~ 10^4; in pipelines dosing 5-50 ppm; polymer chains mechanically degrade in pumps, limiting lifetime to hours.
effects.limits: Mechanical degradation (chain scission) demands continuous reinjection; works only in turbulence - useless in laminar flow; the ~80% asymptote cannot be exceeded; polymer/surfactant cost and possible fouling; surfactant systems lose effect above their cloud temperature.
effects.source: Virk, P.S., Drag reduction fundamentals, AIChE Journal (1975), DOI 10.1002/aic.690210402; classic: Toms, B.A., Proc. 1st Int. Congress on Rheology, North-Holland (1948)

effects.name: Magnetohydrodynamic Pumping (MHD)
effects.description: An electric current passed through a conducting liquid (molten metal, electrolyte, plasma) in a transverse magnetic field experiences Lorentz force f = j x B that pumps the fluid with no moving parts, no seals and no contact; conversely, melt motion in a field induces braking currents (EM braking of casting streams).
applications: Electromagnetic pumps for radioactive liquid sodium in fast reactors (no seal on hot metal)
EM stirring and level control of molten steel and aluminium in continuous casting
MHD braking and shaping of metal streams in casting (contactless gate)
Ship MHD thrusters (Yamato-1 demonstrator) and plasma MPD thrusters
Aluminium electrolysis interface stabilization by magnetic fields
effects.quantitative: Force density f = j x B; Hartmann number Ha = B*L*sqrt(sigma/eta) > 10 flattens the velocity profile; industrial sodium pumps deliver 0.1-10 m3/min at 0.1-0.5 MPa with zero mechanical contact; induced braking can stop melt jets of ~1 m/s in mold-level control.
effects.limits: Requires electrically conductive fluid (oils, most organics excluded; electrolytes give low efficiency <10%); strong fields (0.1-1 T) and high currents needed; electrode corrosion in DC pumps; MHD instabilities in plasma and liquid-metal blankets.
effects.source: Shercliff, J.A., A Textbook of Magnetohydrodynamics, Pergamon Press (1965); classic: Hartmann, J., Hg-Dynamics I, Det Kgl. Danske Videnskabernes Selskab (1937)

effects.name: Fluidized Bed
effects.description: Upward gas flow through a powder bed above the minimum fluidization velocity suspends the particles so the bed behaves like a boiling liquid: it flows, levels, mixes intensely and offers enormous gas-solid contact area at nearly uniform temperature.
applications: Fluid catalytic cracking (FCC) - the backbone of oil refining
Circulating fluidized bed boilers with in-bed desulfurization (limestone addition)
Fluidized-bed CVD coating of granules (silicon, nuclear fuel kernels)
Wurster coating and drying of tablets and powders in pharma
Dry separation of mixed plastics and coal cleaning by density in fluidized beds
effects.quantitative: Minimum fluidization velocity 0.01-1 m/s for 100 um-2 mm particles; bed expands 20-100%; heat transfer to immersed surfaces 200-600 W/(m2*K), ~10x empty-tube gas convection; pressure drop equals bed weight per unit area (independent of flow above Umf); FCC riser velocities 6-20 m/s.
effects.limits: Erosion and attrition of particles and internals; elutriation of fines requires cyclones; bubbling causes gas bypassing (uneven contact); agglomeration and defluidization at high temperature (eutectic melting); unsuitable for sticky or very wide size distributions.
effects.source: Kunii, D., Levenspiel, O., Fluidization Engineering, 2nd ed., Butterworth-Heinemann (1991)

effects.name: Acoustic Streaming (Rayleigh Streaming)
effects.description: Absorption of acoustic energy in a fluid (or viscous loss in the Stokes boundary layer near walls) produces steady second-order vortices that pump and stir the fluid without any moving parts - from sonicator-scale currents to microfluidic particle steering.
applications: Megasonic cleaning of semiconductor wafers (0.8-1 MHz, boundary-layer streaming flushes loosened particles)
Acoustofluidic micro-pumps and mixers for lab-on-chip
Enhanced mass transfer in electroplating and membrane degassing
Thermoacoustic engines and refrigerators (streaming-driven heat transport)
Localized agitation in ultrasonic baths and sonochemical reactors
effects.quantitative: Stokes boundary layer thickness delta = sqrt(2*nu/omega) ~ 1.8 um at 100 kHz and 0.6 um at 1 MHz in water; streaming velocities scale with acoustic intensity: mm/s-scale vortices for W/cm2 fields at MHz frequencies in microchannels; second-order effect (velocity ~ v_acoustic^2/c).
effects.limits: Weak at low intensity (quadratic in amplitude); high frequencies are absorbed within short distances; geometry-dependent (standing waves); fluid heating is a byproduct; competes with acoustic radiation forces on particles.
effects.source: Lighthill, J., Acoustic streaming, Journal of Sound and Vibration (1978), DOI 10.1016/0022-460X(78)90388-7; classic: Rayleigh, L., The Theory of Sound, Macmillan (1878)

effects.name: Hydrodynamic Lubrication
effects.description: Relative motion of surfaces over a converging gap entrains fluid and builds a pressure film (Reynolds equation, 1886) that fully separates them: no solid contact, wear vanishes and the friction coefficient falls to 0.001-0.01 - a self-generating fluid bearing from motion alone.
applications: Journal bearings of turbines, generators and crankshafts (self-pressurizing oil wedge)
Air foil bearings in oil-free turbocompressors and microturbines (air as lubricant)
Squeeze-film dampers for rotor vibration control
Air bearings and Bernoulli grippers in semiconductor lithography stages (contactless wafer transport)
Hydroplaning analysis (the harmful inverse case for tire design)
effects.quantitative: Friction coefficient 0.001-0.01 versus 0.1-0.5 for dry sliding; minimum film thickness 10-100 um in power turbines; peak oil-film pressures 5-30 MPa; air-bearing gaps 5-20 um with stiffness ~10^5-10^6 N/m; regime set by the Sommerfeld number So = (eta*N/P)*(R/c)^2.
effects.limits: Needs relative speed - the film collapses at standstill (start-stop wear; hydrostatic jacking required); film failure under overload, starvation or oil thinning (shear heating); requires converging geometry and mostly laminar regime; narrow gaps are contamination-sensitive.
effects.source: Reynolds, O., On the theory of lubrication and its application to Mr. Beauchamp Tower's experiments, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society (1886), DOI 10.1098/rstl.1886.0005

effects.name: Slush Hydrogen (Densified Two-Phase Cryogen)
