effects.description: A pumpable two-phase mixture of solid hydrogen particles in liquid hydrogen combines the transportability of a liquid with ~16% higher density and ~18% higher cooling capacity per liter than normal-boiling LH2 - the highest volumetric energy density cryofuel, and a general pattern of dual-phase cryogenic working media.
applications: Aerospace propellant densification for launch vehicles and hypersonic craft (NASP studies)
Cryogenic heat sink for scramjet cooling (higher heat capacity per liter)
Slush nitrogen as cooling medium for superconducting equipment and HTS cables
Buffered energy storage between triple and boiling points of cryogens
effects.quantitative: Hydrogen triple point 13.8 K, 7.04 kPa; at ~50% solid mass fraction density is 81.4 vs 70.8 kg/m3 for LH2 (+16%) and available cooling capacity +18%; particles 0.1-2 mm produced by freeze-thaw or auger methods; remains pumpable through standard cryogenic loops.
effects.limits: Aging: particles agglomerate and stratify, requiring re-mixing or circulation; two-phase quantity gauging is difficult (no clean level signal); triple-point vacuum insulation required; filter clogging by solid particles; same safety envelope as LH2 plus solid handling.
effects.source: Verfondern, K., Safety Considerations on Liquid Hydrogen, Forschungszentrum Julich, Energie & Umwelt Vol. 10 (2008), ISBN 978-3-89336-530-2

effects.name: Hall Effect
effects.description: A voltage transverse to current flow arises in a conductor or semiconductor placed in a magnetic field, proportional to the product of current and magnetic flux density
applications: Contactless position and speed sensors (crankshaft, brushless motor commutation)
Non-invasive DC/AC current clamps and meters (mA to kA)
Magnetic field probes from mT to tens of tesla
Proximity and level switches (fuel tanks, door locks)
Flow meters (magnetic-inductive) and e-bike/throttle sensing
effects.quantitative: V_H = I*B/(n*e*t); raw Hall elements give ~10-300 mV/T at rated bias; with on-chip amplifier resolution to ~1 mT; galvanically isolated current sensing from mA to kA; quantum Hall resistance standard R_K = h/e^2 = 25 812.8 Ohm
effects.limits: Weak signal for small fields (needs amplification); offset drift with temperature and mechanical stress; below ~0.1 mT flux concentrators are required; cross-sensitivity to stray fields; not suitable for measuring field gradients with a single element
source: Popovic, R.S., Hall Effect Devices, 2nd ed., IOP Publishing (2004)

effects.name: Wiegand Effect
effects.description: A twisted and aged Vicalloy wire with magnetically hard shell and soft core flips its magnetization in one large Barkhausen jump at a fixed field threshold, inducing a standardized voltage pulse in a coil with no external power
applications: Self-powered rotation and position sensors (camshaft, crankshaft, pedals)
Water, gas and electricity meter registers (multi-decade counting)
Energy harvesting pulses to wake ultra-low-power electronics
Anti-tamper seals, access cards and safe locks
effects.quantitative: Pulse amplitude ~2-12 V, width ~10 us, energy ~0.1-1 uJ per flip; polarity and amplitude independent of field rate; typical operating range -40...+125 C; zero standby power
effects.limits: Threshold event signal only (no analog field value); tiny output energy cannot power continuous electronics; requires magnet + coil assembly; pulse amplitude drifts a few percent with temperature; one pulse per half-revolution max
source: US Patent 3,820,090 'Bistable magnetic device' (Wiegand & Velinsky, 1974)
Sensors (MDPI) 20(5), 1408 (2020), DOI: 10.3390/s20051408 (Wiegand sensor pulse review)

effects.name: Electrostriction
effects.description: All dielectrics deform proportionally to the square of the applied electric field, giving polarity-independent strain used in precision actuators with far less hysteresis than piezoceramics
applications: Deformable mirrors for adaptive optics and laser beam shaping
Nanometer-precision positioning stages (fine motion in STM/AFM-class instruments)
Micropumps and inkjet pump elements
Hydrophone and accelerometer sensing elements
effects.quantitative: Strain proportional to E^2; PMN-based ceramics reach ~0.1% (1,000 ustrain) at 1-3 kV/mm; hysteresis typically <1-2% vs 10-20% for PZT; response below 1 ms
effects.limits: Quadratic law requires DC bias for linear analog control; equal displacement needs higher fields than PZT; response strongly temperature-dependent near phase transitions; high capacitance means large drive currents; low force output (stiffness-limited)
source: Uchino, K., Ferroelectric Devices, CRC Press (2000)

effects.name: Electrostatic Adhesion / Chucking
effects.description: Electrostatic attraction between a biased electrode and an object through a dielectric (or via slightly conductive Johnsen-Rahbek contact) clamps objects without mechanical contact, even in vacuum and plasma
applications: Semiconductor wafer chucks inside vacuum/plasma processing chambers
Pick-and-place of thin glass, foil and film in display manufacturing
Electrostatic holding of paper sheets in copiers and printers
Electrostatic grippers and wall-climbing robots
Dust and sample capture in space research
effects.quantitative: Bias 50 V-3 kV; holding pressure ~1-100 kPa (Johnsen-Rahbek type several times stronger than pure Coulomb type); release within ms at zero bias; works through thin dielectrics and in vacuum where suction cups fail
effects.limits: Force collapses on conductive, dusty or humid surfaces; needs flat clean dielectric contact; residual charge slows release; arcing risk at high voltage in plasma; weak on thick insulators without electrode access
source: Cross, J.A., Electrostatics: Principles, Problems and Applications, Adam Hilger (1987)

effects.name: Electrophoresis
effects.description: Charged particles and macromolecules migrate in a fluid under an electric field at velocities set by their charge-to-size ratio, enabling high-resolution separation and directed deposition
applications: DNA and protein separation/sequencing (capillary and gel electrophoresis)
Electrophoretic deposition (EPD) of ceramic and composite coatings
E-ink displays moving charged pigment particles
Cathodic dip priming (cataphoresis) of car bodies
Zeta-potential characterization of colloids
effects.quantitative: Mobilities ~10^-9 to 10^-7 m^2/(V*s) for macromolecules and typical ions; capillary fields 100-500 V/cm give up to 10^6-10^7 theoretical plates; resolution to 1 bp in DNA fragments; deposition mass proportional to charge passed (Faraday law)
effects.limits: Requires conductive medium; Joule heating caps the usable field in gels; pH and ionic strength shift mobility; objects must carry stable charge; electroosmotic flow can dominate capillaries; uncharged particles do not respond
source: Tiselius, A., 'A new apparatus for electrophoretic analysis of colloidal mixtures', Trans. Faraday Soc. 33, 524 (1937)

effects.name: Electric Arc / Thermal Plasma
effects.description: A self-sustained high-current discharge produces ionized gas at 6,000-25,000 K, concentrating extreme heat and chemical reactivity in a small steerable volume
applications: Arc welding and plasma cutting of metals
Plasma spraying of wear and corrosion coatings
Electric arc furnaces melting scrap steel
Arc lamps and plasma torches for waste gasification
Plasma chemistry: nanoparticle synthesis, ozone production
effects.quantitative: Arc core 6,000-25,000 K; currents 1 A to 100 kA; power density 10^6-10^8 W/m^2 at electrode spots; plasma jet velocity 1,000-5,000 m/s in cutting torches
effects.limits: Electrode erosion and acoustic/EMI noise; UV and ozone hazard; arc wander needs magnetic stabilization; very high power consumption; unsuitable for heat-sensitive substrates; plasma chemistry products hard to predict
source: Roth, J.R., Industrial Plasma Engineering, Vol. 1: Principles, IOP Publishing (1995)

effects.name: Induction Heating
effects.description: Alternating magnetic fields drive eddy currents directly inside conductive workpieces, heating them contactlessly, even through a furnace wall or crucible
applications: Surface hardening of gears and shafts at controlled depth
Vacuum induction melting and crucible heating
Brazing, soldering and shrink-fitting assemblies
Induction cooktops and adhesive drying
Float-zone refining of semiconductor silicon
effects.quantitative: Frequencies 50 Hz-10 MHz; skin depth delta = 503*sqrt(rho/(mu_r*f)) m (Cu: ~9 mm at 50 Hz); surface heating rates above 1,000 K/s; hardening depth 0.5-5 mm at 10-400 kHz; overall efficiency 50-90% depending on coupling
effects.limits: Only conductive workpieces; ferromagnetic heating vanishes above the Curie point; complex 3D shapes need engineered coils; high-frequency power electronics costly; stray fields heat nearby metal parts
source: Zinn, S. & Semiatin, S.L., Elements of Induction Heating: Design, Control and Applications, ASM International (1988)

effects.name: Eddy Currents / Skin Effect
effects.description: Time-varying magnetic fields induce closed-loop currents in conductors that oppose field change, the basis of contactless testing, braking, and confinement of AC current to a surface layer
applications: Eddy-current NDT of cracks, wall thickness and conductivity
Eddy-current brakes and dampers (trains, rides, vibration damping)
Metal sorting and induction cooktop heating
Litz wire and RF design accounting for skin depth
Electromagnetic forming and stirring of melts
effects.quantitative: Skin depth in Cu: ~9.2 mm at 50 Hz, ~65 um at 1 MHz; ECT detects surface cracks ~0.1-0.5 mm; eddy braking force grows with speed (self-limiting, no wear); penetration tunable 0.1-10 mm via frequency
effects.limits: Only conductive materials; poor sensitivity to deep/subsurface defects; lift-off and edge effects mask signals; permeability variations in ferromagnets mimic defects; braking ineffective at low speed
source: Yavorsky, B.M. & Detlaf, A.A., Handbook of Physics (Справочник по физике), Nauka (1968)

effects.name: Magnetic Levitation
effects.description: Magnetic forces - active attraction (EMS), induced repulsion (EDS), or diamagnetic/superconductor expulsion - suspend bodies without solid contact, eliminating friction and wear
applications: Maglev trains (Transrapid EMS, SCMaglev EDS)
Frictionless bearings for flywheels, turbomachinery and pumps
Magnetic suspension balances and microgravity simulation
Contactless positioning and stirring of molten metals
Levitated displays and kinetic art with active stabilization
effects.quantitative: EMS air gap ~10 mm (Transrapid, active control bandwidth ~kHz); EDS gap ~100 mm with superconducting coils; SCMaglev speed record 603 km/h (2015); Earnshaw's theorem forbids stable static levitation of ferromagnets - needs active feedback, induced currents, diamagnets or superconductors
effects.limits: Earnshaw instability rules out passive ferromagnetic levitation; active systems fail if sensors/power fail; strong stray fields near SC coils; eddy losses heat the guideway in EDS; cryogenics and cost for superconducting versions
source: Moon, F.C., Magneto-Solid Mechanics, Wiley (1984)

effects.name: Electric Double-Layer Capacitor (Supercapacitor)
effects.description: Ions electrostatically adsorbed at enormous electrode/electrolyte interfaces (no chemical reaction) store charge in an ultra-thin double layer, giving millions of cycles and extreme power density
applications: Regenerative braking buffers (trams, buses, cranes, forklifts)
Backup power for memory, clocks and smart meters
Peak-power shaving in hybrid drivetrains and wind pitch systems
Buffer storage for intermittent harvesters (solar, Wiegand, vibration)
Grid frequency regulation modules
effects.quantitative: Capacitance 1-3,000 F per cell (large cells to ~10,000 F) from 1,000-3,000 m^2/g activated carbon; energy 5-10 Wh/kg (hybrid types to ~30); power up to 10^4 W/kg; cycle life 500,000-1,000,000; -40...+65 C; cell voltage ~2.7 V
effects.limits: Energy density 10-20x below Li-ion; linear voltage discharge needs DC-DC conversion; electrolyte decomposition caps cell voltage ~2.7 V; self-discharge over days; high cost per stored kWh
source: Conway, B.E., Electrochemical Supercapacitors: Scientific Fundamentals and Technological Applications, Kluwer/Plenum (1999)

effects.name: Photoelectric Effect
effects.description: Photons above a threshold energy liberate electrons from matter (external effect) or excite electron-hole pairs across a semiconductor bandgap (internal effect), converting light directly into electricity
applications: Solar cells and photovoltaic modules
Photomultiplier tubes detecting single photons
Photodiodes and CCD/CMOS imaging arrays
Automatic lighting, exposure meters, optical interrupters
Spectrophotometry and quantum optics foundations
effects.quantitative: Work functions 2.1 eV (Cs) to ~5 eV (Pt); Si bandgap 1.12 eV gives 1,107 nm cutoff; Shockley-Queisser limit 33.7% for a single junction at 1 sun; commercial Si modules 20-23%, lab Si record ~27%; PMT gain 10^6-10^8
effects.limits: Threshold law: photons below work function/bandgap are useless; Si output drops ~0.4%/C; dust and partial shading cut current disproportionately; external effect needs vacuum and clean surfaces; single-junction physics caps efficiency
source: Einstein, A., 'Uber einen die Erzeugung und Verwandlung des Lichtes betreffenden heuristischen Gesichtspunkt', Ann. Phys. 17, 132-148 (1905)

effects.name: Photoconductivity
effects.description: Illumination raises a semiconductor's free-carrier population, dropping its resistance by orders of magnitude, so light becomes an electrical switch without any mechanical contact
applications: Photoresistors (LDR) and twilight/dusk switches
Xerography: OPC or Se drum discharge writes the latent image
Flame and smoke detectors sensing IR flicker
Optically triggered power semiconductors (photo-SCR/LTT)
Photodetectors from visible to IR (CdS, PbS, CdHgTe)
effects.quantitative: Dark-to-lit resistance change 10^2-10^6; CdS LDR: Mohm dark to a few kohm at 100 lux; response from ns (photodiodes) to 10-100 ms (CdS); spectral range tunable via bandgap 0.1-3 eV
effects.limits: Slower and more temperature-drifting than photodiodes; memory/latency after bright exposure; Cd compounds toxic (RoHS exceptions needed); not energy-converting (needs bias); saturates at high illumination
source: Bube, R.H., Photoconductivity of Solids, Wiley (1960)

effects.name: Luminescence (Fluorescence / Phosphorescence)
effects.description: Substances emit light after UV, electron or photon excitation, with nanosecond lifetimes (fluorescence) or long afterglow (phosphorescence) set by spin selection rules - distinct from bioluminescence which is a living-organism chemical reaction
applications: LED phosphors (YAG:Ce) and display color conversion
Fluorescent tracers for leak detection and flow visualization
Security inks, UV banknote marks, forensic luminol
Glow-in-the-dark emergency signage (SrAl2O4:Eu,Dy)
Scintillators for X-ray and gamma detection
effects.quantitative: Fluorescence lifetimes 0.1-10 ns; phosphorescence 1 ms to >10 h; Stokes shift 20-100 nm; good phosphor quantum yields ~0.9; fluorescein detectable at ~0.1-10 ug/L by fluorimetry
effects.limits: Photobleaching and fatigue of organic dyes; quenching by oxygen, heat and impurities; excitation needs a matched UV/blue source; rare-earth cost and supply; afterglow decays hyperbolically rather than staying constant
source: Blasse, G. & Grabmaier, B.C., Luminescent Materials, Springer (1994)

effects.name: Photochromism
effects.description: Reversible light-induced isomerization switches a molecule between two states of different color/absorption, combining an optical memory and a self-regulating filter in one molecule
applications: Self-darkening eyeglass lenses (AgX glass, naphthopyrans)
UV dosimeters and chemical actinometers
Rewritable optical data storage and molecular switches
Smart privacy films and optical filters
Document authentication marks
effects.quantitative: Glass lenses darken in 30-60 s in sun and fade in 1-5 min; diarylethene switching ns-ps; organic fatigue 10^4-10^6 cycles; AgX glasses endure >10^5 darken/fade cycles
effects.limits: Thermal relaxation erases many written states within minutes; fatigue limits lifetime; too slow for video-rate displays; dark state temperature-dependent; write/erase needs two different wavelengths
source: Durr, H. & Bouas-Laurent, H., Photochromism: Molecules and Systems, revised ed., Elsevier (2003)

effects.name: Bragg Diffraction / Photonic Bandgap (FBG Sensor)
effects.description: Periodic structures with pitch Lambda selectively reflect the wavelength satisfying lambda = 2n*Lambda; in fiber Bragg gratings the reflected wavelength shifts with strain and temperature, turning the grating into a distributed sensor
applications: FBG strain/temperature sensor arrays embedded in bridges, pipelines, composite blades
X-ray crystallography of crystals and proteins
WDM filters and narrow-line fiber laser reflectors
Photonic-crystal LEDs and VCSEL mirrors
Acousto-optic tunable filters
effects.quantitative: lambda_B = 2*n_eff*Lambda; FBG sensitivity ~1.2 pm/ustrain and ~10 pm/C at 1550 nm; interrogator resolution 0.1-1 pm gives ~0.1 ustrain; dozens of gratings multiplexed on one fiber over km; standard gratings anneal above ~300 C (regenerated/type II survive to ~800 C)
effects.limits: lambda_B responds to BOTH strain and temperature (needs compensation element); senses only along the grating; photonic crystals require nm-precision fabrication; narrowband reflection needs many elements for broadband work
source: Yablonovitch, E., Phys. Rev. Lett. 58, 2059 (1987), DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.2059
Hill, K.O. et al., Appl. Phys. Lett. 32, 647 (1978), DOI: 10.1063/1.89881 (first fiber Bragg grating)

effects.name: Laser Interferometry
effects.description: Two coherent beams recombined into fringes turn sub-wavelength optical path differences into countable light-dark transitions, measuring displacement at nanometer scale without touching the object
applications: Nanometer positioning of lithography wafer stages
Laser vibrometers and TV-holography vibration mapping
Optical surface testing (Fizeau, Twyman-Green)
Gravitational wave detection (LIGO-class interferometers)
Gauge block calibration and precision dilatometry
effects.quantitative: One fringe = lambda/2 ~ 316 nm (He-Ne 633 nm); heterodyne interferometers reach 0.1-1 nm resolution over meters; LIGO detects 10^-19 m displacements on 4 km arms; ranges up to tens of meters
effects.limits: Needs a coherent stable laser and clean optics; air turbulence and temperature drift the refractive index; ambiguity at lambda/2 without counting; requires reflective or semi-transparent surfaces; vibration isolation needed at precision
source: Hariharan, P., Basics of Interferometry, 2nd ed., Academic Press (2007)

effects.name: Laser Ablation
effects.description: Focused laser pulses vaporize or eject material layer by layer; ultrashort fs/ps pulses remove matter faster than heat can diffuse, giving cold machining with micron and sub-micron precision
applications: Refractive eye surgery (LASIK/ReLEx) at ~0.25 um per pulse
Laser cleaning of artworks, rust and molds without abrasives
Drilling cooling holes in turbine blades and PCB microvias
Pulsed laser deposition of thin films and nanoparticles
LIBS elemental analysis of the removed plasma
effects.quantitative: Fluence thresholds 0.1-10 J/cm^2; removal 10 nm-1 um per pulse; fs pulses confine heat (pulse < electron-phonon time) giving heat-affected zone <0.1-1 um; intensities 10^8-10^13 W/cm^2; features below 1 um
effects.limits: Reflective or transparent materials scatter the energy (wavelength must match absorption); plume redeposition and debris; low throughput for large volumes; optics contamination; ns-pulse thermal mode still melts polymer edges
source: Bauerle, D., Laser Processing and Chemistry, 4th ed., Springer (2011)

effects.name: Selective Absorption / Spectrometry
effects.description: Every molecule and atom absorbs at a fingerprint set of wavelengths; measuring which wavelengths are absorbed, and how strongly, identifies and quantifies substances remotely and non-destructively
applications: NDIR CO2/CH4 gas analyzers and HVAC sensors
Atomic absorption / ICP-OES trace metal analysis at ppb
Stack gas and automotive emission monitoring
NIR moisture and authenticity control in food/pharma
Astronomical spectroscopy of stellar composition
effects.quantitative: Beer-Lambert law A = eps*c*l; AAS/ICP detection limits 0.1-10 ug/L; atomic absorption lines ~0.002 nm wide; NDIR CO2 at 4.26 um resolves ~1 ppm; NIR moisture precision to 0.01%
effects.limits: Overlapping bands in mixtures need chemometrics; scattering and turbidity fake absorption; calibration standards and drift compensation required; path length matters; fails on opaque or strongly scattering media
source: Ingle, J.D. Jr & Crouch, S.R., Spectrochemical Analysis, Prentice Hall (1988)

effects.name: Optical Tweezers
effects.description: A tightly focused laser beam traps dielectric particles in the intensity maximum through gradient and scattering forces, holding and moving micro-objects with piconewton forces and zero mechanical contact
applications: Single-molecule force spectroscopy (DNA stretching, motor proteins)
Cell sorting and manipulation without damage
Assembly of microstructures and photonic crystals
Measuring adhesion and viscoelasticity of soft matter
Raman trapping for identifying airborne or suspended cells
effects.quantitative: Forces 0.1-100 pN; traps dielectric particles ~10 nm to ~100 um; position detection to ~1 nm; force calibration to ~0.01 pN; typical laser 0.5-2 W at 1,064 nm (low water absorption)
effects.limits: Object refractive index must exceed the medium; absorption heats and kills biological samples; forces too small against flows faster than mm/s; diffraction limit on trap size; needs a transparent optical path
source: Ashkin, A., Dziedzic, J.M., Bjorkholm, J.E. & Chu, S., Opt. Lett. 11, 288 (1986), DOI: 10.1364/OL.11.000288

effects.name: TiO2 Photocatalysis
effects.description: UV light on titanium dioxide creates electron-hole pairs that generate hydroxyl radicals oxidizing organic pollution into CO2 and water, while the surface turns superhydrophilic - the surface cleans itself
applications: Self-cleaning glass, tiles and facade coatings
Air purification: NOx, formaldehyde and VOC decomposition
Water treatment and antibacterial surfaces
Fujishima-Honda water splitting toward hydrogen
Self-cleaning textiles and solar panel coatings
effects.quantitative: Anatase bandgap 3.2 eV needs lambda < 387 nm; hydroxyl radical redox potential +2.8 V (above ozone); superhydrophilic contact angle < 5-10 deg after UV exposure; thin organic films decompose over hours-days of sunlight
effects.limits: Needs UV (only ~3-5% of sunlight); electron-hole recombination without defect engineering; activity fades from fouling and aging; too slow for thick contamination; airborne TiO2 nanoparticles raise inhalation concerns
source: Fujishima, A. & Honda, K., Nature 238, 37 (1972), DOI: 10.1038/238037a0

effects.name: Catalytic Combustion
effects.description: A Pt/Pd catalyst oxidizes fuel at its surface at a few hundred degrees instead of a 1,500 C+ flame - the same heat with orders of magnitude less thermal NOx and flameless safety
applications: Catalytic gas heaters (flameless, safe for confined spaces)
Gas-turbine catalytic combustors with single-digit ppm NOx
Automotive three-way catalytic converters
VOC oxidation in industrial exhaust air
Domestic catalytic cookers and hand warmers
effects.quantitative: Light-off 250-350 C vs flame 1,400-1,900 C; thermal NOx forms above ~1,500 C, so catalytic burners emit <5-20 ppm NOx; three-way catalysts convert 98-99+% of HC/CO/NOx; methane ignition lowered by ~200-300 C
effects.limits: Poisoning by S, Pb, Si compounds; sintering deactivates above ~900 C; needs preheat to light-off; pressure drop across the monolith; Pt-group metal cost; fuel slip if overloaded
source: Pfefferle, W.C. & Pfefferle, L.D., 'Catalytically stabilized combustion', Prog. Energy Combust. Sci. 12, 25-41 (1986), DOI: 10.1016/0360-1285(86)90012-2

effects.name: Electrochemical Machining / Electropolishing
effects.description: Anodic dissolution in an electrolyte removes metal atom by atom at a rate independent of hardness - shaping superalloys with no tool wear, no burrs and no heat-affected zone
applications: Turbine blade and blisk shaping from Ni/Co superalloys
Deep complex cooling holes in hardened steel
Deburring of cross-drilled hydraulic components
Electropolishing of pharma/food-grade stainless surfaces
Pulsed ECM micromachining of medical implants
effects.quantitative: Current density 10-500 A/cm^2; Faraday removal ~2.2 cm^3 per 1000 A*min for iron (efficiency ~1); surface Ra 0.1-1.6 um; tolerances +/-0.02-0.1 mm; works on 60+ HRC alloys; zero tool wear
effects.limits: Only electrically conductive workpieces; electrolyte handling, corrosion and disposal (NaCl/NaNO3); large DC power demand; tool cathode design is case-specific; possible hydrogen pickup requires baking for fatigue-critical parts
source: McGeough, J.A., Principles of Electrochemical Machining, Chapman & Hall (1974)

effects.name: Anodizing
effects.description: Electrolytic oxidation grows the metal's own oxide into a controlled porous layer - thickness set by voltage (~1.3 nm/V) - that hardens, protects, insulates and accepts dyes
applications: Hard anodized wear surfaces (pistons, gears, aerospace parts)
Decorative colored aluminum for architecture and electronics housings
Corrosion protection of marine and aviation aluminum
Insulating dielectric in electrolytic capacitors
Porous alumina templates for nanostructure fabrication
effects.quantitative: Barrier layer ~1.2-1.4 nm/V; decorative films 5-25 um, hard anodizing 25-100 um at 350-550 HV; sealed coatings pass 336 h+ salt spray; pore diameter 10-30 nm; thick hard coats reduce Al fatigue strength if unsealed
effects.limits: Works mainly on valve metals (Al, Ti, Ta, Zr); oxide grows partly inward so dimensions change; porous layer is brittle under impact; high-Si/dark alloys anodize unevenly; part size limited by bath and rectifier
source: Keller, F., Hunter, M.S. & Robinson, D.L., 'Structural features of oxide coatings on aluminum', J. Electrochem. Soc. 100, 411 (1953)

effects.name: Passivation / Corrosion Inhibition
effects.description: A nanometer-thin oxide or adsorbed inhibitor film blocks the anodic reaction, dropping corrosion current by orders of magnitude - protection with grams of additive instead of kilograms of coating
applications: Stainless steel Cr2O3 self-passivation and nitric acid pickling
Benzotriazole-type inhibitors for copper cooling loops
Sacrificial Mg/Zn anodes and impressed-current protection
Phosphate/chromate-free conversion coatings under paint
Concrete rebar inhibitors and surface sealers
effects.quantitative: Passive film on stainless 1-3 nm thick; inhibitors work at 10-100 ppm with 90-99% efficiency; corrosion current reduction 10^2-10^4; steel protection criterion -0.85 V vs Cu/CuSO4 (Mg anodes drive ~-1.5 V)
effects.limits: Passivity breaks down in hot chloride media (pitting above ~60 C); inhibitors are medium-specific and increasingly regulated (chromates banned); sacrificial anodes need renewal; films damaged by abrasion or acid; Pourbaix predictions assume equilibrium
source: Uhlig, H.H. & Revie, R.W., Corrosion and Corrosion Control, 3rd ed., Wiley (1985)

effects.name: Hydrogen Embrittlement
effects.description: Atomic hydrogen diffusing into high-strength metals accumulates at defects and slashes ductility, so parts fracture at loads far below design strength days or years after exposure (delayed failure)
applications: Bake-out treatments after plating/pickling (prevention)
Material hardness limits in sour oil & gas service (NACE MR0175)
Hydrogen-economy pipeline and vessel design
Failure analysis of bolts, springs and fasteners
Low-hydrogen welding practice (basic-coated electrodes)
effects.quantitative: High risk above ~1,000 MPa tensile strength (or >39 HRC); cracking possible at 30-70% of yield; H diffusivity in pure alpha-iron ~10^-9 m^2/s at RT (far lower in steels due to trapping); standard relief baking 190-220 C for 4-24 h; NACE hardness cap 22 HRC
effects.limits: Mainly steels/Ti/Ni alloys - Al and Cu nearly immune; needs atomic hydrogen (molecular H2 diffuses slowly at RT); failures are statistical and hard to predict; no reliable NDT before cracking; competing mechanisms (HEDE/HELP) still debated
source: Gangloff, R.P. & Somerday, B.P. (eds.), Gaseous Hydrogen Embrittlement of Materials in Energy Technologies, Woodhead Publishing (2012)

effects.name: Self-Healing Polymers
effects.description: Microencapsulated monomer plus dispersed catalyst (or reversible bonds and vascular networks) polymerizes inside a crack as it forms, autonomously restoring most of the strength without human repair
applications: Crack-healing epoxy composites in aerospace structures
Self-healing anticorrosion coatings that reseal at scratches
Automotive clearcoats repairing swirl scratches via reversible bonds
Self-healing concrete admixtures (capsules, bacteria)
Extended-life wind-turbine blade matrices
effects.quantitative: White et al. (2001): 50-200 um DCPD microcapsules + Grubbs catalyst recovered 75% of fracture toughness; modern systems reach 80-100% (single cycle); vascular networks heal 3-7+ times; fatigue life extended severalfold
effects.limits: Capsule systems heal once (capsule consumed); Grubbs catalyst is expensive and air-sensitive; room-temperature healing works only for selected chemistries; capsules degrade virgin stiffness; large cracks exceed the delivered healing volume
source: White, S.R. et al., 'Autonomic healing of polymer composites', Nature 409, 794-797 (2001), DOI: 10.1038/35081973

effects.name: Hydrogel Swelling
effects.description: Cross-linked polymer networks absorb many times their weight in water and swell reversibly; sensitivity to pH, temperature or ions turns the volume change into a soft actuator, sensor or absorber
applications: Superabsorbent diapers and agricultural water reservoirs
Soft grippers and artificial muscles (pH/T-responsive)
Drug delivery matrices releasing by swelling and diffusion
Soft contact lenses (38-75% water content)
Water-blocking swellable seals in cables and construction
effects.quantitative: Superabsorbent polymers take up 30-1,000 g water per g dry polymer (diapers 30-60 g/g); PNIPAM collapses above LCST 32 C; swelling pressure up to ~1 MPa; volume change 10-1,000%; response seconds-hours (diffusion-limited)
effects.limits: Slow kinetics (diffusion scales with t^2); very low strength when swollen; deswelling slower than swelling; hysteresis and fatigue over cycles; dries out in arid environments; not load-bearing
source: Wichterle, O. & Lim, D., 'Hydrophilic gels for biological use', Nature 185, 117-118 (1960), DOI: 10.1038/185117a0

effects.name: Adsorption / Zeolite Molecular Sieves
effects.description: Crystal lattices with pores of precisely 0.3-1 nm and huge internal surface sort molecules by size and polarity, drying gas to deep dew points and separating air with pressure swings instead of heat
applications: Deep drying of air and refrigerants (dew point to -60 C and below)
PSA oxygen concentrators delivering 90-95% O2 from air
Solvent recovery and VOC capture on activated carbon
Shape-selective catalysis (ZSM-5/MFI in refining)
CO2 capture on 13X and amine-modified sieves
effects.quantitative: Pore windows: 3A 0.30 nm, 4A 0.38 nm, 5A 0.50 nm, 13X ~1.0 nm; zeolite surface 500-700 m^2/g (activated carbon 800-1,500); H2O capacity up to 20-25 wt%; equilibrium dew points below -60 C; PSA cycle ~60 s to minutes
effects.limits: Capacity falls sharply with temperature (needs regeneration heat/vacuum); poisoning by oils and siloxanes; friable and dusty; selectivity is thermodynamic so tricky for azeotrope-like pairs; cycling attrition generates fines
source: Breck, D.W., Zeolite Molecular Sieves: Structure, Chemistry and Use, Wiley (1974)

effects.name: Sintering / Powder Metallurgy
effects.description: Particles pressed and heated to 0.6-0.9 of the melting temperature bond by surface diffusion and capillarity, densifying into net-shape parts - with engineered residual porosity as a bonus function
applications: Self-lubricating porous bronze bearings (oil-impregnated)
Cemented carbide cutting tools (WC-Co)
Metal injection molding of complex small parts
Additive manufacturing (SLM/SLS/DMLS)
Sintered filters, wicks and heat-pipe capillary structures
effects.quantitative: Sintering T = 0.6-0.9 T_m; final density 92-99.5%; linear shrinkage 15-25%; MIM tolerances +/-0.1-0.3%; WC-Co hardness 1,300-1,800 HV; residual porosity 15-30% for self-lubrication
effects.limits: Residual porosity cuts fatigue and toughness vs wrought metal; shrinkage complicates tolerances; expensive dies suit batches only; some alloys hard to atomize; trapped gas pores degrade properties; furnace size limits part dimensions
source: German, R.M., Sintering: From Empirical Observations to Scientific Principles, Butterworth-Heinemann (2014)

effects.name: Explosion Welding
effects.description: A controlled detonation slams plates together at a grazing angle; the metal jet scours surfaces clean and atomic bonding welds even metal pairs that fusion welding cannot join
applications: Clad steel: Ti, stainless or Al sheets bonded on steel for vessels and heat exchangers
Al-steel and Cu-steel transition joints for shipbuilding and electrochemistry
Repair sleeves on pipelines
Joining dissimilar metals without brittle intermetallics
Large bimetallic electrical contacts and busbar transitions
effects.quantitative: Detonation velocity 2,200-3,000 m/s; collision angle ~5-20 deg; bond strength at least that of the weaker parent; clad plates up to ~20 m^2; wavy interface typical; contact lasts microseconds so heat-affected zone is minimal
effects.limits: Lap-type joints only (plates, tubes), needs standoff distance; noise and blast rules demand remote sites; wavy zone can harden or crack hard metals; thin foils difficult; limited to simple flat/cylindrical geometries
source: Crossland, B., Explosive Welding of Metals and its Application, Clarendon Press, Oxford (1982)

effects.name: Martensitic Quench Hardening
effects.description: Quenching traps steel's carbon by a diffusionless shear transformation to body-centered tetragonal martensite, jumping hardness to 55-67 HRC with ~1-4% volume expansion as a side effect - distinct from shape-memory martensite which is engineered to be reversible
applications: Hardening bearings, gears and cutting tools (55-67 HRC)
Case hardening of carburized gear teeth
Spring, armor and rail steel processing
Martensitic stainless knives and scalpels
Distortion-controlled martempering and ausforming
effects.quantitative: Critical cooling rates 10^2-10^6 K/s (hardenability-dependent); martensite hardness 55-67 HRC at 0.4-0.9% C; volume expansion ~1-4%; retained austenite up to ~30% if quench insufficient; tempering at 150-650 C restores toughness
effects.limits: Quench cracks and distortion from thermal gradients; must temper immediately after quench; thick sections cool too slowly inside (hardenability limit); high-carbon martensite is brittle; quench oils are fire and disposal hazards
source: Krauss, G., Steels: Processing, Structure, and Performance, ASM International (2005)

effects.name: Amorphous Metals / Metallic Glasses
effects.description: Alloys cooled faster than crystallization can nucleate (or engineered at deep eutectics) freeze into a glassy solid with no grain boundaries, ~2% elastic strain (10x steel) and yield strength up to 5 GPa
applications: Amorphous transformer cores (core loss ~1/3 of Si-steel)
Watch cases, phone hinges and luxury goods (scratch-proof + springy)
Surgical instruments and needle tips (sharp and elastic)
Golf club faces and sports equipment
Micro-gears and parts by thermoplastic forming near Tg
effects.quantitative: First alloys needed 10^5-10^6 K/s (thin ribbons); bulk metallic glasses (Zr-, La-, Mg-based) cast at 1-100 K/s into cm-scale parts; elastic limit ~2% (vs 0.2% steel); yield strength up to 5 GPa; hardness 500-1,000 HV; softening near Tg enables forming
effects.limits: Brittle at room temperature (no dislocation plasticity) - limited structural use; critical casting thickness caps part size to cm; expensive elements (Zr, Be in Vitreloy); difficult to weld or join; shear-band localization causes sudden fracture
source: Klement, W., Willens, R.H. & Duwez, P., 'Non-crystalline structure in solidified gold-silicon alloys', Nature 187, 869-870 (1960), DOI: 10.1038/187869b0

effects.name: Giant Magnetoresistance (GMR)
effects.description: In magnetic multilayers the relative alignment of adjacent layer magnetizations swings resistance by tens of percent; spin-dependent scattering became the read head of the information age
applications: HDD read heads (areal density growth ~100%/yr after 1997)
GMR magnetometers and automotive wheel-speed sensors
MRAM memory cells (with MTJ/TMR variants)
Biosensing of magnetic nanoparticle labels (immunoassays)
Dirt-immune rotary encoders
effects.quantitative: Baibich et al.: delta-R/R ~50% at 4.2 K in Fe/Cr at 4 T; room-temperature spin valves 5-15% at <10 mT; read heads sense fields of a few mT; Nobel Prize 2007 (Fert & Grunberg); TMR tunnel junctions exceed 200%
effects.limits: Needs nm-perfect multilayers (sputtering, vacuum tech); hysteresis from layer switching; temperature drift; fields beyond saturation erase the signal; ESD kills spin-valve stacks
source: Baibich, M.N. et al., 'Giant magnetoresistance of (001)Fe/(001)Cr magnetic superlattices', Phys. Rev. Lett. 61, 2472 (1988), DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.61.2472

effects.name: Corona Discharge
effects.description: At sharp electrodes the local field exceeds air breakdown and a quiet glow of non-thermal plasma forms, generating ions and ozone that charge, precipitate and chemically transform at kilovolts with only microamp current
applications: Electrostatic precipitators cleaning flue gas (99-99.9% of fly ash)
Xerography/printing: drum charging and toner transfer
Ozone generation for water and air disinfection
HV-line condition monitoring (corona loss, audible noise, UV cameras)
Ionizers for static neutralization and air cleaning
effects.quantitative: Onset when local field exceeds ~3x10^6 V/m (a few kV on needle tips); ESPs remove 99-99.9% of particles; currents uA-mA at 5-100 kV; non-thermal - the bulk gas stays near ambient temperature
effects.limits: Produces ozone and NOx (indoor health hazard); energy-inefficient for chemistry; limited current before streamer-to-spark transition; electrode fouling degrades performance; humidity shifts onset voltage and ozone yield
source: Loeb, L.B., Electrical Coronas: Their Basic Physical Mechanisms, University of California Press (1965)

effects.name: Electroluminescence
effects.description: Electric field or carrier injection directly excites light emission in phosphors and semiconductor junctions - solid-state light with nanosecond response and no filament or gas discharge
applications: LED lighting (100-200 lm/W commercial, 300+ in labs)
Displays: OLED, micro-LED and EL backlight panels
Status indicators, automotive and traffic signaling
Optocouplers and IR emitters for remote controls
EL wire and panels for low-power signage
effects.quantitative: Commercial LED efficacy 100-200 lm/W; blue GaN internal quantum efficiency >80%; switching ns-us; AC EL panels driven at 40-300 V with 10,000+ h life; blue GaN LED Nobel Prize 2014 (Akasaki, Amano, Nakamura)
effects.limits: Efficiency droop at high current density; heat and phosphor thermal quench; EL panels dim over lifetime; white light needs phosphors/QDs for color mixing; OLED lifetime uneven across colors (blue shortest)
source: Schubert, E.F., Light-Emitting Diodes, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press (2006)

effects.name: Multilayer Insulation (MLI)
effects.description: Nested radiation shields — alternating reflective foils and spacers in vacuum — cut radiative heat flux roughly in proportion to 1/(n+1) for n shields; the Dewar vessel is the two-shell ancestor. Canonical implementation of TRIZ nested-structure principle combined with vacuum (taking-out).
applications: Cryogenic tanks and LNG storage
Spacecraft thermal control (JWST sunshield)
Superconducting magnet Dewars
Vacuum flasks and cold chains
effects.quantitative: effective thermal conductivity ~0.1–1 mW/(m·K) at high vacuum (still air ~25 mW/(m·K)); heat flux ≈ q₀/(n+1) for n identical reflective shields; typical layer density 10–30 layers/cm; losses grow steeply with compression (empirically ~N³·⁵)
effects.limits: needs high vacuum — gas conduction kills the effect; compression, seams and penetrations dominate real heat leaks; moisture degrades reflectivity
effects.source: NASA SP-8003 (1965). Multilayer Insulation Systems; Tien, C.L., Cunnington, G.R. (1973). Cryogenic Insulation Heat Transfer. Advances in Heat Transfer, 9
